author: Unknown
title: [Paris/Montreuil] Les 16 et 17 octobre 2026 contre la torture en prison
content:
Les 16 et 17 octobre 2026, le collectif anticarcéral de L'Envolée invite à un week-end de discussions contre les

QLCO

 (quartiers de lutte contre la criminalité organisée) : de nouveaux quartiers de haute sécurité qui durcissent encore l'appareil répressif. L'Envolée et ses invité.es– ancien·nes prisonnier·es, proches, militant·es associatif·ves, avocats... – proposent de faire entendre la voix sans cesse réduite au silence des prisonnier·es, pour comprendre ensemble de quoi la prétendue «

 

guerre au narcotrafic

 

» est vraiment le nom, et pour imaginer ensemble les moyensde lutter contre les

QLCO

.


Torture de l'isolement poussée à l'extrême, déshumanisation des prisonniers et des proches, surveillants cagoulés en permanence : tel est le quotidien dans ces quartiers ouvertement destinés à faire souffrir le plus possible.


Dès leur ouverture, prisonniers et proches ont cherché à faire entendre par tous les moyens qu'un cap avait été franchi en termes de torture carcérale. Malgré la rigueur du dispositif, les prisonniers se sont organisés collectivement (communiqués, blocages, grèves de la faim, recours juridiques).


En fait, c'est le sort de tous les prisonnier·es qui dépend de ces bagarres contre les

QLCO

, car les pratiques mortifères de ces quartiers sont déjà en train de contaminer toutes les autres prisons.


Tandis que dehors on parle de fascisation, les prisonniers des

QLCO

 et leurs proches vivent déjà le fascisme.


Se battre à leurs côtés, c'est lutter contre le glissement de toute la société.

author: Unknown
title: Analyse und Learnings von Wald statt Schutt und Wald statt Repression
content:
Die Kampagne rund um die Rümlanger Waldbesetzung und die darauf folgende Repression hat nun rund 3 Jahre gedauert. Schlussendlich waren es viele kleine bis grössere Erfolge, die eingefahren werden konnten. Wir wollen nun zurückschauen und insbesondere unsere Learnings teilen – Learnings über anarchistische Organisation, Kampagnenstrategien und Solidarität und Support bei unerwartet grosser Repression.


Kontext


Im April 2023 besetzen einige Aktivist*innen unter dem Namen “Wald statt Schutt” den Rümlanger Wald nahe der Zürcher Stadtgrenze. Der Wald sollte abgeholzt werden, um die Schuttdeponie nebenan zu erweitern. Die Schuttdeponie, wo unsere Wohnhäuser landen, welche der Gentrifizierung zum Opfer fallen. Die Besetzung war gleichzeitig ein Ort der gelebten Autonomie und Utopie.


Nach zwei Wochen wurde die Besetzung mit einem riesigen Polizeiaufgebot geräumt. In der Folge wurde gegen Besetzende und Unterstüzende, welche in der Nähe des Waldes kontrolliert wurden nicht nur ein Strafverfahren gestartet (Strafrecht), sondern die Polizei wollte ihnen die Einsatzkösten verrechnen (Verwaltungsrecht) und die Eigentümer*innen des Waldes ihren Aufwand (Zivilrecht).


In der Folge startete die Kampagne “Wald statt Repression” mit zwei zentralen Zielen:


1. Die Betroffenen zu Unterstützen in der riesigen Repression dieser 3 Rechtsfällen und die damit verbundenen absurd hohen Kosten.


2. Ein Präzedenzfall schaffen, dass die Überwälzung von Polizeieinsatzkosten nicht mit den Grundrechten vereinbar ist.


Strafrecht: Die Vorwürfe bezüglich den angeblichen Verstössen gegen das Waldgesetz und Sachbeschädigung endete schon auf der Stufe Bezirksgericht mit klaren Freisprüchen. Nur Personen die nicht freiwillig von den Bäumen herunter kamen wurden zu je 100.- Franken Busse aufgrund “Nicht befolgen einer polizeilichen Anweisung” verurteilt.


Zivilrecht: Die absurd hohen Rechnungen der Waldeigentümer*innen bleiben unbezahlt. Und Gegen die darauf folgenden Betreibungen wurde Rechtsvorschlag eingelegt. Nach den Freisprüchen im Strafrechtsfall zogen die Waldeigentümer*innen die Zivilforderungen nicht weiter.


Verwaltungsrecht: Die Polizeikostenüberwälzung wurde vom Verwaltungsgericht aufgrund fehlender Gesetzesgrundlage zurückgewiesen. Es hat jedoch verpasst darüber zu urteilen, ob eine Polizeikostenüberwälzung an sich grundrechtswidrig ist.


Im November 2025 hat auch das Baurekursgericht den Erweiterungsplan als rechtswidrig erklärt und somit die Deponieerweiterung blockiert. Dieses Urteil wird momentan aber von den Deponie-Betreiber*innen weitergezogen. Auch an der Abriss- und Gentrifizierungspolitik der Staat ZuReich hat sich noch nichts geändert. Die Kämpfe gehen weiter!


Ausführlichere Updates findet ihr hier:


https://barrikade.info/article/5846


https://barrikade.info/article/5969


https://barrikade.info/article/6078


https://barrikade.info/article/7274


https://barrikade.info/article/7342


Wald statt Schutt – Rodung verhindert, Gentrifizierung verdrängt weiter


Die Kernaussage der Kampagne Wald statt Schutt war: “Die Gentrifizierung in der Stadt ist sowohl unsozial, wie auch naturzerstörerisch”. Das Ziel: Brücken bauen. Wir wollten die Menschen in den Themen abholen, die Ihnen wichtig sind und Zusammenhänge zu weiteren Problematiken aufzeigen. Den Ökos zeigen, dass diese seltenen Käfer und wertvollen Ökosysteme nicht aus einfacher Ignoranz zerstört werden, sondern dass die Immobilienspekulation, die Profitgier des Immobiliensektors und die Skrupellosigkeit der Zement- und Bauindustrie, nicht nur Tiere und Pflanzen, sondern auch Menschen aus ihren Lebensräumen verdrängen und beides Teil des selben Problems ist. Aber auch den Städter*innen zu zeigen, dass ihre Verdrängung auch mit der Zerstörung ausserhalb der Stadt zusammenhängt.


Die Vielzahl der Kampaganen-Narrative war dazu da, ein diverses Sprektrum an Menschen abzuhohlen, was teilweise gelang. Sowohl Teile aus der autonomen, revolutionären Linken, als auch bürgerlichen NGOs oder Privatpersonen konnten sich anschliessen oder zumindest solidarisieren. Hingegen war es für einige Personen auch schwierig uns einzuschätzen, aufgrund dieses Spagates.


Zum Rümlanger Wald sind wir auch immer wieder auf andere Akteur*innen zugegangen, welche sich für den Erhalt des Waldes eingesetzt haben. Das waren NGOs, ein Bürger*innen-Komitee und Lokalpolitiker*innen. Und wir sind überzeugt, dass die Rodung des Waldes nur verhindert werden konnte, weil sich all diese verschiedenen …

author: Jummai Bulama-Ashebu
title: Who started Nollywood?
content:
Here is the short version of a story that has been told wrong for 30 years.

Kenneth Nnebue was born in Mgbidi, Imo State. He left school after sixth grade and apprenticed under his brother, a handbag maker, before entering trade himself in the Onitsha market. By the late 1980s, he was in Lagos, importing VHS tapes from Taiwan, distributing pirated foreign films, and trying to move product in a difficult economy. When the tapes stopped selling, he put an original story on them instead. That story —

Living in Bondage

 (1992) — cost 150,000 naira, about $7,000 at the time. It sold over 100,000 copies in its first weeks through informal markets in Lagos, Enugu, and beyond. It launched a global industry.

What gets left out of most tellings: before Nnebue made

Living in Bondage

 in Igbo, he had already produced at least 27 Yoruba-language films. An Igbo trader, operating in Lagos, making Yoruba content, who then made the Igbo film the world decided was the beginning of everything. The ethnic ownership of that origin — who gets to claim Nollywood, which tradition gets the credit, which city gets the heritage tourism — has been contested ever since. Not because the evidence is unclear, but because resolving it requires someone to say plainly what Nollywood actually is: an art form rooted in Yoruba theatrical tradition, or an industry born from an Igbo trader’s logistics problem. These are different things. The confusion between them is not innocent.

The Yoruba side of the argument is not a retroactive claim. The Yoruba Traveling Theater tradition,

Alárìnjó

, reaches back to the 19th century. Its modern form is usually traced to Hubert Ogunde, whose touring theater company toured Nigerian cities through the 1950s and 1960s, its work politically sharp enough that a regional premier banned it outright. That stage tradition migrated to celluloid film through the 1970s and 1980s, and by 1985 Moses Olaiya’s

Mosebolatan

 was one of the country’s first genuine blockbusters. Critically, Yoruba filmmakers moved onto VHS format in 1988, four years before

Living in Bondage

. If the question is who touched the video format first, it wasn’t Nnebue.

So why does his name carry all the credit? Because

Living in Bondage

 wasn’t first, but it was the first to look like it knew what it was doing, packaged with a glossy, full-color cover styled after pirated Hollywood tapes, presented as a professional product instead of a stopgap. The story helped too — a man who joins an occult society and sacrifices his wife for wealth, only to be haunted by what he’s done — landed hard in a country deep in structural adjustment-era desperation, when stories of ritual money were part of the cultural air people breathed. And despite being shot entirely in Igbo with no subtitles for a full year, the film crossed ethnic lines anyway — co-producer Okey Ogunjiofor would later say simply that people who didn’t understand the language still understood the story, because the pictures carried it.

What Nnebue actually contributed, then, wasn’t the invention of video filmmaking — Yoruba practitioners had that four years earlier. He contributed a “template,” an industrial model of direct-to-video production that the entire industry would replicate for the next two decades. Every straight-to-video Nollywood film that followed, regardless of language, was built on the business logic Nnebue stumbled into while solving an unglamorous warehouse problem.

Laid side by side, these two histories aren’t actually contradictory; they’re answering two different questions. It’s the single phrase “who started Nollywood” that collapses them into one, forcing a false contradiction. The Yoruba lineage answers where the art form came from. The Nnebue story answers where the industry came from. Ogunde’s company built the grammar. Nnebue’s warehouse problem built the factory.

I’m writing this from Enugu, one of the cities where

Living in Bondage

 first sold by the hundreds in market stalls. Here, Nollywood’s Igbo roots aren’t distant history but lived memory, passed down the way a family recipe is. That memory is real. So is Ogunde’s banned theater company. Neither one needs to lose for the other to be true.

But Nigeria rarely lets cultural origin stay this generous. Who started Nollywood is never just a historical question here — it’s tied to tourism revenue, festival programming, whose language gets state funding, whose grandchildren get to say “we built this.” …

author: Oyugi Abednego Ochillo
title: Whose Kingdom Is It? Religion and Power in Kenya
content:
In June 2026, Burkina Faso’s Transitional Legislative Assembly

passed a law

 giving the state new powers to license and monitor religious worship. Weeks later, Captain Ibrahim Traore told Burkinabe students studying Sharia in Saudi Arabia that they need not come home, framing the choice of what to study abroad as

a question of national loyalty

. A government that can suspend preaching and threatens someone’s citizenship over a course of study has decided that religious authority is, at bottom, a security problem, something to be licensed, monitored and disciplined from above.


Kenya is fighting a version of the same battle from the opposite direction, and from below rather than above. During the 2024 Finance Bill protests, young Kenyans

accused

 churches of accepting political donations while remaining silent as the state used force against demonstrators, and told clergy to return the money before expecting to regain anyone’s trust. Where Traore reached for a decree, Gen Z reached for a demand addressed straight at the pulpit. That is the more interesting fight, because it is being waged through persuasion and public shame rather than law, which makes it slower and messier, but also more honest about what accountability from a religious institution should actually look like. Burkina Faso is useful here only as the outer edge of what state control of religion can become. From here, this piece stays in Kenya.


My argument is that Kenya’s churches, particularly the Pentecostal and charismatic institutions that dominate the country’s religious economy, have built a financial and political relationship with the state that Gen Z is now the first generation to seriously question from inside the pews rather than from outside them. Paul Gifford’s scholarship explains the theology that made this relationship possible. William Ruto’s conduct since 2024 shows exactly how a sitting president exploits it. A small number of clergy and lay institutions are demonstrating, unevenly, what it would actually take to break the pattern.


The question Gen Z is actually asking is not abstract, and it deserves to stand largely in the protesters’ own words rather than mine. “I’m here because our country’s money is being misused,” one protester told reporters outside Jesus Winner Ministry in June 2025, days after President Ruto

donated

 twenty million shillings to that same congregation. Occupy Church’s own organizer,

Mwabili Mwagodi

, put the same challenge more bluntly to the churches themselves: “Where is this money coming from? Bring us the receipts.” Even some of the clergy have started to frame the comparison the same way. In his 2025 Ash Wednesday homily, Nakuru’s Catholic Bishop Cleophas Oseso

warned

 that congregations should not be seen accepting political donations while “schools have no books and hospitals have no medicine”. That was the actual framing of the question. Not a general complaint about corruption in the abstract, but a direct comparison between what a single Sunday donation cost and what an unfunded clinic or classroom costs the same week.


The economics of miracle and tithe


Harambee

 itself is not the problem. It began as a genuine communal practice, neighbours pooling money for school fees or a hospital bill, and much of it still works that way at the level of a village or a church congregation raising funds for a borehole. What changed is scale and direction. Once national politicians discovered that a

harambee

 podium could double as a campaign stage, the same word came to describe a president handing over millions of shillings in a single televised gesture, and the distance between those two things is most of what this argument is trying to name.


Paul Gifford’s decades of

research

 on Kenyan Christianity describe how the prosperity gospel replaced older forms of church accountability with a direct transaction between believer and preacher. A pastor promises breakthrough, healing, or business success. The believer gives, often well beyond what they can afford, because the sermon has recast giving itself as the mechanism of the miracle. The old model, where a congregation could hold a church leader to account because it funded him collectively, gets replaced by something closer to a bet. Gifford’s sharper point, the one that matters for this piece, is what that bet does to politics rather than to individual believers. Once poverty is read as a spiritual test rather than a policy failure, a …

author: Dina A. Mohamed
title: Beyond useless guilt and insatiable victimhood
content:
In 2018, my first year living in Amsterdam, studying for a master’s degree in the arts, I went to a museum to attend a performance by a group of queer artists addressing questions of injustice. The setting seemed familiar enough until one of the presenters announced that anyone who did not belong to specified “marginalized identities” should leave the room. They began reading a list of those identities aloud.


For a moment, I just listened, suspended, trying to locate myself in the list. Then it became clear: the list excluded non-queer, white people. I, therefore, “belonged.” I found that the category I best fit in was “woman of color,” a definition I had never once used for myself at that time.


I stayed. The conversation turned to safety in the Netherlands, to harassment and violence connected to skin color, gender identity, sexual orientation. The others spoke from experience I could hear but not share. Amsterdam, for me, had been something else entirely: quiet nights walking alone through streets I did not know, a strange lightness I had no name for yet. No one had stopped me. No one had read me by my color. I am not denying that such violence exists, only that it had not, at that point, been my story.


And so, I said nothing.


That moment stayed with me. It crystallized something I had been sensing since arriving in Europe: a pressure, felt everywhere in public discourse, to read every experience through the lens of identity. To locate yourself on a map drawn by others and then speak only from that location.


What unsettled me was not the artists’ choice to create a protected space. It was the underlying logic, one I kept encountering: in seminar rooms, in cultural institutions, in the language of activist circles. A logic by which identity is constructed entirely on the axis of oppression: one group over another, history compressed into a single narrative, and every human being assigned a fixed position within it. You are either a victim or a perpetrator. There is no third position. The space between is simply erased. 


When pain becomes a pass


When being a victim is the only position that confers moral authority, the only place from which you are permitted to speak without being immediately questioned or condemned, then victimhood stops being a condition and starts becoming a currency. And currency, by nature, is something people reach for.


But to understand why this happens so readily today, you have to look at the broader cultural atmosphere in which identity politics operates. 


We live, as sociologist Frank Furedi argued in

Therapy Culture:


Cultivating Vulnerability in an Uncertain Age

(Routledge, 2004), in a society that has undergone a profound redefinition of what a person is.

 Clinical language such as trauma, triggers, nervous system dysregulation, safe spaces and emotional damage has migrated out of the therapy room and into everyday speech, political discourse and social media. The effect is that vulnerability has become the defining feature of how people understand themselves and others. To be a person, in this framework, is first and foremost to be at risk, to be potentially harmed, to be in need of recognition for your wounds. The self is constituted around its injuries.


This matters because it explains the ease with which therapeutic self-diagnosis feeds into political victimhood. When the culture already teaches you to understand yourself primarily through the prism of what has damaged you, and when the cultural framework simultaneously grants moral authority only to those who have been damaged, the two systems reinforce each other seamlessly. It offers people a coherent identity, a community, a moral position and a language, all at once. What it does not offer, and what it actively erodes, is agency. Therapeutic culture places people in a permanent state of recovery rather than transcendence: you are instructed to acknowledge your wounds endlessly and to identify yourself with and through them. Applied to politics, this means suffering becomes not something to be overcome collectively but, in a twisted way, something to be performed and preserved because it is the source of your standing.


Philosopher

Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò

 put it plainly: “pain — whether borne of oppression or not — is a poor teacher. Suffering is partial, short-sighted, and self-absorbed. We shouldn’t have a politics that expects different: oppression is not a prep school”. This is a difficult thing to …

author: Ahmed Ogwell Ouma
title: Ebola and Africa’s Preparedness Dividend: From Crisis to Capability
content:
Africa is facing its 17

th

 Ebola outbreak, and this time the continent is meeting it with the most capable response architecture it has ever assembled. The outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was declared on 15

th

 May 2026, and both WHO and Africa CDC have classified it as a public health emergency. The

Bundibugyo strain

 in circulation is one of four Ebola virus species that infect humans, and it has no licensed rapid diagnostic, therapeutic or vaccine. The system that catches and contains it is African-built, African-run, and African-coordinated, and it is working.


This African capability is fifty years in the making, however, the financing that built it and was sustaining it is now severely constrained. National health budgets in Africa have not yet met the 15% threshold set by the

Abuja Declaration on HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis and other Related Infectious Diseases in 2001

, while Overseas Development Assistance (ODA) for health continues to drop. Whether the next pandemic is contained quickly will depend on whether the architecture designed over time is maintained and functional.


The benefits of past investments are undeniable. Outside the 2014 to 2016 West Africa epidemic,

which reached 28,600 cases

, no Ebola outbreak this century has exceeded 5,000 cases, and most have been below 500. Uganda’s 2022

Sudan-strain outbreak

 was contained in under four months. The turning point was the West Africa epidemic, which

killed more than 11,000 people

 and forced the institutional reforms that now define the response, such as Africa CDC

becoming operational in 2017

, the

rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine

 reaching the market, and national public health institutes being strengthened across the continent.


The architecture of success


1. Frontline workforce


Ebola outbreaks end at community level where they begin, in homes, care settings, and burial practices. The WHO has set the standards for

risk communication and community engagement

 since the first Ebola outbreaks in 1976. The work is delivered by community health workers, transporters, and traditional and religious leaders. In DRC, VillageReach trains these cadres and provides technical assistance to the

Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (COUSP)

. This is the operational interface between the formal surveillance system and the communities where outbreaks emerge, and it is what makes the rest of the architecture function successfully.


2. Sample transport and laboratory turnaround


A case confirmed within 24 to 48 hours with follow-up action stops most onward transmission. A case confirmed in

 several weeks, as was the case in West Africa in 2014

, gives the virus time to seed in different communities. Across 15 Africa countries including the DRC, VillageReach has developed an efficient and effective transport network that shifts into emergency fast-track when an outbreak alert is raised. In 2025, we further strengthened this in DRC by adding a

new laboratory in Mweka

 to shorten the journey from the source. The infrastructure that stops outbreaks is the same one that operates before an outbreak is detected. Containment succeeds when dual-use systems are continuously maintained, not activated only in emergencies.


Dr. Christian Ntumba, a medical biologist from the National Public Health Institute in DRC, collecting Ebola blood samples from the treatment center to send to the laboratory for testing Ituri Province, DRC. Photo Credit: Josué Kumbi


3. Surveillance


During my time at Africa CDC, I saw firsthand how much effort went into building surveillance systems capable of detecting outbreaks before they become emergencies. That investment is now paying dividends. Today, the

event-based surveillance

 framework now operates in

two-thirds of African Union member states

. National public health institutes in DRC, Uganda, Nigeria, and Kenya have built

integrated surveillance systems that did not exist a decade ago

. The

7-1-7 framework

, now widely adopted in global preparedness, sets clear benchmarks – seven days to detect a threat, one day to notify authorities and seven days to mount an effective response. The difference is not technical capacity but proximity. Surveillance works when communities are part of the system, identifying and reporting threats early. Surveillance fails when the first signal reaches institutions only after an outbreak has gained momentum, turning what could have been contained locally into a …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: ‘Like ICE’: Western Cape police accused of unlawfully detaining foreign migrants
content:
Up to 200 foreign migrants have been in detained by the police since the 30

th

 of June as part of the state response to the anti-immigration protests led by March and March and Operation Dudula. The Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration declared even before the xenophobic deadline that the arrest of “illegal foreign nationals” would be intensified.


The Western Cape Coalition Against Xenophobia (WCC-AX) is raising the alarm over the conduct of the South African Police Service in Robertson and surrounding towns, which it likens to that of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE) of the United States of America. ICE is is carrying out the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign, often arresting migrants in public places and immigration offices. They have killed 8 immigrants and protesters this year, with over 50 detainees dying since 2025.


WCC-AX say that the rights of the migrants have been trampled upon as they languish in jail in Robertson and surrounding Winelands towns, denied medication, their basic sanitary requirements, and food. They are all from our neighbouring states, mostly Zimbabwe, and Malawi, Mozambique and Lesotho.


The Robertson police denied these claims and said food brought by relatives and supporters of the detainees has been allowed, but access has to be managed. “The station commander has confirmed that food brought by relatives is permitted, subject to a controlled process, and that visits are allowed but managed due to the large number of family members seeking access to detainees,” said the police.


But the police are not managing the acceptance of goods as it is arbitrary, with some police officers refusing and others being sympathetic to the plight of the detainees, WCC-AX responded. “The acceptance of goods,  including medication, has been totally arbitrary, with some police simply refusing to accept items, going so far as to say they ‘don’t care’, while other police have acknowledged this pattern and acted differently, but all entirely at their own discretion apparently.”


Sheriff Ramaobi, an activist in the area, confirmed that they were told that they cannot bring anything to the detainees. “One of our colleagues who visited one of the prison cells in Robertson asked these questions in terms of, can we bring medication or food supplies to our migrant brothers and sisters?  And it was denied. Other police stations, like McGregor and Montagu, strictly said that we’re not allowed. We are not allowed to give any support to the people that are incarcerated,” she said.


The police also deny that the detainees have been kept in jail illegally, saying that they have acted within the law and in cooperation with the Department of Home Affairs. “The foreign nationals detained for immigration-related purposes are dealt with in terms of the applicable legislation and in cooperation with the Department of Home Affairs, which is responsible for immigration administration and deportation processes,” said SAPS.


WCC-AX disputes this, saying that after they paid the admission-of-guilt fines, they were supposed to be released and not kept in jail for over two months. “If the police wanted to continue to detain them, they should have followed the administrative procedures laid down in s34 of the Immigration Act. The law states that people have to be told why they are being detained and what their rights are, including their right to challenge the deportation decision and to legal representation. Their continued detention must come before a court with them getting the opportunity to make representations. This did not happen. That’s why their continued detention is unlawful,” WCC-AX argues.


Anti-immigrant protesters outside the provincial legislature in Cape Town on the 30

th

 of June. File photo by Mzi Velapi


WCC-AX demands


The key demands of the Western Cape Coalition Against Xenophobia include the release of the detainees, for SAPS members to “stop acting like members of March and March (and ICE in the US)”, and act within the law.


The anti-xenophobia group is also calling for the suspension of police officers accused of failing to enforce the law and human rights violations, and that they must be subjected to an inquiry. The South African Human Rights Commission must also conduct an investigation. “The minister of home affairs must explain why his departmental officials conflate criminal and administrative proceedings in contravention of the Immigration Act,” …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: The “Rape Tournament”: Online Humour and Normalisation of Rape Culture in Namibia
content:
Between April 2024 and February 2025, Namibia recorded

 4,405 cases


of gender-based violence (GBV), of which 1,345 were cases of rape. These figures may not reflect the actual prevalence, as many incidents, particularly in rural communities, remain unreported due to persistent barriers to reporting. The most recent shocking case happened in June when a


25-year-old

 woman was gang raped at knife point by nine minors aged between 15 and 17. The news spread widely across social media, and with it came a violent


discourse

.

 One might expect that such dark and painful news would spark empathy, outrage, and solidarity. Instead, the news was met with many jokes, victim-blaming, sexual objectification, and open mockery of the survivor. These online comments are not merely insensitive humour. It is a disturbing display of how sexual violence is normalised and reveals social evidence of a broader rape culture in Namibia.


When Rape Becomes a “Tournament”


The title of this article emerged

from w

hat unfolded in the Facebook comment sections where the case, in effect, turned into a “rape tournament.”  At the dawn of the news, Namibians on Facebook rephrased this incident from a crime to sports, competition, and masculine camaraderie. In

this

Facebook discourse, the 9 suspects lined up in the photo like a football team, sparking sports references. A significant proportion of users, predominantly male, mocked the incident, curious about who the

“man of the match”

 was and who

“kicked the first penalty”.

 They further referred to the assault as a

“round-robin tournament,”

all of which transformed this violent crime into a public spectacle. 


This discourse appeared to erase the criminal and dehumanising act and reduced the survivor’s trauma to jokes and entertainment. Thus, the “rape tournament” term is used deliberately not to sensationalise the crime, but to describe how many commenters collectively reframed gang rape as though it were a sporting event. These comments construct an entirely different narrative about the survivor and perpetrators. She is no longer portrayed as a survivor of violence. She is rather signified as a playing field upon which the “match” occurred. This, in turn, frames the perpetrators as players whose acts are evaluated, celebrated, and compared. This shows that the football jokes were not isolated comments but formed a pattern.  


The social media comment section acts as a cultural space in which violence is publicly rehearsed, reinforced and legitimised.


The humour masked the true horror of the assault. When rape becomes a tournament, it sustains the rape culture in Namibia. Sexual violence alone does not sustain rape culture; it is also fed by the everyday attitudes, language, and habits that excuse, downplay, or normalise these acts. At its core, these Facebook comments show exactly how humour is used as a tool to keep rape culture alive and well in online spaces.


Victim Blaming Masked as Safety Concerns


Victim-blaming

 rarely appeared in explicit form. It was masked as “safety advice,” in which commenters framed their responses as concern for women’s safety. A significant number of people questioned why she was out that late at night,

with

one male user cautioning all women to stay indoors as soon as the streetlights go on to protect themselves. Women were advised not to walk at night, not to make unnecessary movements after dark

.

 One female commenter even suggested that the survivor should have remained at the home of the man she had allegedly visited and simply endured the “walk of shame” the following morning. At face value, these comments appear protective. However, they subtly relocate responsibility from those who commit violence to those who experience it. The discussion therefore ceases to ask why boys assaulted a woman and instead asks why a woman was outside.


The safety of women in Namibia is a concern given the increasing GBV-related cases in the country. However, the Facebook discussion extended beyond safety concerns and focused predominantly on regulating women’s movements, clothing, relationships and behaviour while remaining largely silent on the conduct of the alleged perpetrators. This kind of talk just aims to control women instead of questioning violent and toxic male behaviour. The burden of preventing sexual violence was therefore relocated from those who commit it to those who experience it. This sheds light on the double standards on …

author: WoMin
title: Wathint’ Abafazi, Wathint’ Imbokodo: Why Challenging Xenophobia Is Unfinished Women’s Business
content:
On 17 August, SADC leaders concluded their 46th summit in Durban, against a backdrop of heightened xenophobic protests, threats, and forced repatriations. August is Women’s Month in South Africa commemorating 70 years since women marched on the Union Buildings fighting against apartheid and pass laws. However, this month has been marred by the recent spate of Afrophobia and xenophobia across the country. SADC’s communiqué recorded an update from South Africa on migration governance and called for coordinated regional dialogue on the drivers of migration. It did not explicitly name xenophobia or Afrophobia — even after months in which Black African migrants have faced intimidation, violence, and pressure to leave South Africa. In an 

Open Letter

 to the SADC Heads of State and Government, WoMin African Alliance, together with The People’s Dialogue, calls for those Heads of State to place xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa on its formal agenda, issue a clear public resolution, and commit to measurable regional action. 


Those 20 000 courageous women across race, class and religion marched on 9 August 1956 to confront the Apartheid regime’s institutionalisation of white supremacy and racial capitalism by controlling Black life and movement. The Pass Laws inscribed that control, requiring pass books at all times, and described Black people as “aliens” and “illegal” in the country of their birth. Sophie De Bruyn, the only living leader at this year’s commemoration, shared “that the freedom we marched and bled for is in reality a painful paradox. How can we celebrate our past victories when our current realities are so deeply disappointing and distressful?”  


The pass laws did not simply restrict movement — they dictated who belonged where, who could work, where they could live, and who counted as fully human within South Africa’s borders.  


This historic day of protest was about fighting for a free, democratic South Africa in which all peoples, regardless of race, class and gender, could be emancipated and live with dignity and equality. Already liberated countries on the continent stood alongside Black South Africans in full solidarity, offering a home, bearing the brunt of economic pressure and military assault, especially for frontline states.  


While the pass laws are painful history, the current reality for Black South Africans falls far short of our freedom dreams. Much of Apartheid endures in lived memory — continued spatial injustice, the deepest economic inequality globally, and more than 33.6% unemployment. 


For WoMin African Alliance, rooted in Pan African feminist politics, this is no coincidence. Women’s Month cannot be commemorated as mere nostalgia — it must be treated as unfinished business. The emergence of Xenophobia and Afrophobia results from deep, intersecting crises in South Africa, as set out in our 

statement

 on Afrophobia and Xenophobia. 


The root cause of this crisis is the neoliberal economic policies implemented by the South African government, along with a long history of racial capitalism in which Black people were exploited for cheap labour to build the economy but have remained economically and politically excluded. What we are witnessing is the crumbling and disintegration of our society. Today, South Africa’s huge unemployment rate represents millions of lives suspended in a state of permanent insecurity. This disintegration has the greatest impact and consequences on Black women. 


Impacts on women

 


Women face the most inequality, earning 23% to 35% less than men for the same work, and accounted for 77% of all job losses in 2025. They are concentrated in low-income, informal, or precarious employment such as domestic work. Women-headed households face a roughly 60% chance of being poor. This places a triple burden on women, who bear most unpaid domestic work and child-rearing — labour unrecognised in national accounts and that hampers their economic advancement. 


These statistics represent structural violence rooted in inequality, patriarchy, social dislocation, and dispossession. Rather than confront the state’s failure to transform the economy and property relations, create decent work, or provide basic services, migrants become easy scapegoats for crises produced by capitalist and neoliberal policy. The unemployed South African is encouraged to blame the Zimbabwean street vendor, the Ethiopian spaza shop owner, or the Somali trader, instead of asking why …

author: Nelly Madegwa
title: Faith, Power, and Paradox in Kenya’s Church
content:
“The Church must not move so close to the state, because you can get burned. The state is like fire. But the Church must also not stay very far from it, because you might feel a lot of cold.” That warning was passed down to Bishop Charles Ong’injo, of the Anglican Church of Kenya’s Maseno South Diocese, by a former archbishop. Balancing that closeness is difficult, he told me. But he was clear about where the danger has historically come from. “Each time the Church has felt very comfortable with the state, then you realize that people suffer,” he said. “If you read the history of revolutions in the world, be it the French Revolution or any other, you realize it was sometimes triggered by the comfort the Church was enjoying from the state.” Get too close to the fire, in other words, and it is not only the Church that gets burned.


I grew up believing the Church was where you went to learn how to live right. I did not expect it would also be where I would learn how easily “living right” could mean staying quiet.


Matthew 10:30 tells us that even the hairs on our head are numbered, a reminder of how closely God is meant to care about our lives. So, church leaders should care about the finance bills that have left many of us drowning in debt, unable to feed, clothe, or house ourselves. They should care that we cannot access healthcare because money meant for hospitals has been misappropriated, or afford school because public money is tied up in corruption scandals that will likely never be resolved.


I eventually found myself in a place I never wanted to be; I did not want to leave my faith, but I also could not remain in the Church. I have seen the sneer on people’s faces when they hear the comment, “I love God, I practise my faith, I just don’t go to church.” I understand. It’s been hard to do one without the other. I hate that I had to leave the Church and try to practise my faith outside of it. But how could I sit and listen to people who did not seem to care about my daily struggles, not as abstract issues, but as things I was actually living through?


I don’t have a roadmap for this. I have felt lost more times than I liked, but there’s still something there.


I do not know how this fits into my journey toward heaven later. With all of this sitting in me, I wanted to talk to someone who had chosen the harder side of that warning rather than simply theorize about it.


If the Church is meant to be close enough to society to know when people are hurting, what is it supposed to do when the country itself is in crisis? Kenya has been living through protests, abductions, and endless corruption scandals. “I think the role of the Church remains constant whether the country is in crisis or not,” Bishop Ong’injo said, “because the Church is the conscience of society. It must constantly remind its citizenry that they have a responsibility to be each other’s keeper, to ensure the rule of law, because our constitution gets its strength from God’s laws. When we are in a crisis, the Church must add its voice to all the other voices championing for justice.”


If the Church was supposed to be society’s conscience, then silence was not neutral. I shared with Bishop Ong’injo what I had noticed in my own church; leaders remaining silent while congregants grew frustrated enough to call them out. Was the burden of demanding a just and fair country ours alone, or did it belong to the people leading us, too? “Spiritual leadership entails that, first of all, you are standing in the gap,” he said, “and a spiritual leader is supposed to stand in the gap between human beings and God. Like the old biblical prophets, they are supposed to warn, warning of the dangers when we are not doing the correct thing. It can be very catastrophic, and therefore, they are not supposed to be reminded by their congregants of what to do, because they are supposed to be listening to the voice of God.”


Bishop Ong’injo illustrated this role with the image of the watchman. “The watchman might not be a soldier who will fight the enemy, but the watchman is supposed to warn that where you are standing is dangerous. The enemy is coming. Can you take cover? And, therefore, sometimes we may not do much, but we must shout like the watchman, because that is what we are called to do. You must warn people that you are in a dangerous situation. Just the way every Sunday we preach against sin, because it destroys life. I think that is a critical role that the Church …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris
title: Sudan Nashra: Hemedti in Addis Ababa | Buildup at Ethiopian base fuels concerns over RSF corridor toward Blue Nile capital, military sends massive reinforcements | RSF fortifies West Darfur capital with berms, reinforces troops | RSF commander in North Kordofan defects, arrives in capital with 200 fighters
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


When Rapid Support Forces Commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo quietly touched down in Addis Ababa last week, the Blue Nile State front was raging along Ethiopia’s border and reinforcements for the fighting were amassing on both sides. Ethiopia, meanwhile, was contending with renewed tensions of its own. 


For the RSF, keeping channels open with Addis Ababa is particularly important given that its border is part of the security environment surrounding the fighting in Blue Nile. Operations and troop movements along the border were among the main subjects of Hemedti’s talks, according to an RSF leadership source and an Ethiopian government source who spoke to Mada Masr. For the Ethiopian source, Addis Ababa’s immediate concern is keeping Sudan’s war from spilling across the border.


But Sudanese intelligence sees another layer to Ethiopia’s interest in the RSF. Ethiopia could factor the paramilitary group into its own military arrangements as it manages conflicts with domestic opponents, particularly amid renewed tensions with Tigray, a Sudanese intelligence source said. Such a relationship could also give Addis Ababa greater room to operate on the Sudanese side of the border, they added.


The Sudanese military is watching that possibility from an increasingly exposed position. It has lost the strategic border towns of Geisan and Kurmuk in Blue Nile and is now trying to stop the advance from the border toward Blue Nile’s capital, Damazin.


And there is a new reason for concern — a significant buildup since July at an Ethiopian military base in

Asosa, located in the Benishangul-Gumuz region bordering Sudan.

 The area has been repeatedly used to launch major operations by the RSF and its allies into Blue Nile. But an intelligence source in the state said the recent buildup could make the cross-border corridor into Kurmuk and Geisan harder for the military to penetrate and could facilitate the unimpeded movement of supplies and forces to the RSF and its allies.


With the border towns secured, the RSF and its allies are now pushing against the military positions guarding Damazin. They captured Bakori in the Geisan locality and Sirkum in Kurmuk last week, triggering a rush of military reinforcements into the state capital and the positions around it.


While the military is shoring up Damazin, the RSF is fortifying Geneina, the capital of West Darfur. Military operations this week secured another position near the city, part of an offensive that has been underway since July and has brought military and allied forces within reach of the RSF-held capital. 


The RSF is now digging around the city, extending sand berms and trenches as a defensive measure against a possible surprise attack. This week, it brought in large numbers of fighters in what a military field source described as preparation for attacks on military positions in West Darfur and neighboring North Darfur.


Kordofan, the war’s critical faultline between an RSF push east and a military push west, saw its second major defection this week. Abu Bakr Dahloub, the RSF’s intelligence chief for special missions in North Kordofan’s Hamra al-Sheikh and the Egypt-Libya-Sudan border triangle, defected to the military with around 200 fighters.


After securing major gains in North Kordofan weeks ago, the military continues to target RSF supply and gathering points in neighboring West Kordofan. Military aircraft struck several fuel and ammunition depots and RSF gatherings there this week, destroying supplies that had just arrived to reinforce positions in the area. 


In Khartoum, the state is trying to get its internal political dialogue off the ground despite intractable disagreements with major political forces over the process itself. The dialogue’s preparatory committee announced its formation this week and is now beginning outreach. But ongoing disputes over the committee’s independence, the fact that talks will be held in military-controlled territory and the question of who gets a seat at the table remain major obstacles to its efforts to secure participation.


***


Hemedti in Addis Ababa


In his second trip to the Ethiopian capital since the war broke out, RSF Commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo arrived in Addis Ababa in an unannounced visit on August 26.


Hemedti’s first visit, in December 2023, was a formal trip that culminated in a political declaration with Abdalla Hamdok, the prime …

author: Kimberly Mabaso
title: Papers, Please: Canon Collins 2026 Essay Shortlisted Finalist
content:
This piece was a shortlisted finalist for the

Canon Collins 2026 essay competition

. The annual competition invites essays that demonstrate thought leadership and offer fresh perspectives on issues affecting southern Africa.


Some of my earliest memories are not of places but of words.


One of those words was

kwerekwere

.


I heard it long before I understood it. It drifted through school corridors and playground conversations, sometimes wrapped in laughter, sometimes sharpened into an insult. As a child, I knew nothing about immigration policies, borders or xenophobia. I only knew that whenever the word was directed at me, it carried a message that was impossible to misunderstand, it said to me “you are not one of us”.


I was two years old when my family moved from Zimbabwe to South Africa. South Africa is where I learned to read and write, where I made friends, where I attended school and imagined a future for myself. It is the country whose streets, accents and seasons shaped my understanding of the world. It is, for all practical purposes, home. Yet there were moments growing up when none of that seemed to matter as much as the place printed on a birth certificate. The older I became, the more I realised that borders do not always exist where we think they do. We imagine borders as fences, checkpoints and lines drawn across maps, but the most enduring borders are often invisible. They appear in conversations. They reveal themselves in assumptions. They emerge when someone asks where you are really from, as though your first answer could not possibly be enough. They surface whenever a person is reduced to their nationality before they are recognised as a human being.


My earliest encounter with this reality came when I was six years old. Xenophobic violence had erupted in parts of South Africa. Years later, newspapers would describe the attacks in terms of immigration, politics and public unrest. My memory is much simpler. I remember sleeping at the beach with my family because it felt safer than sleeping at home. I remember the uneasiness of the adults around me and the strange awareness that something had changed, even if I could not yet understand what it was. Children rarely understand the reasons behind fear, they simply absorb it. Looking back, what unsettles me most is not the violence itself but the ideas that made it possible. Violence does not begin with burning shops or broken windows. By the time those things happen, something deeper has already taken root. It begins in the stories people tell about who belongs and who does not. It grows whenever human beings are transformed into problems to be solved rather than neighbours to be known.


In recent years, South Africa has once again witnessed a rise in anti-immigrant sentiment. Foreign nationals are routinely blamed for unemployment, crime and failing public services. Faced with complex social and economic challenges, it is often easier to point to visible outsiders than to confront more difficult realities. Yet what I find particularly striking is how little legality seems to matter. Public debates often suggest that the issue is documentation, that hostility is directed only at those who lack the proper papers. Yet lived experience tells a different story. Refugees carrying valid permits, students lawfully enrolled at universities and long-term residents who have spent years contributing to their communities often find themselves subjected to the same suspicion. Recent anti-immigrant campaigns and protests have only reinforced this reality, demonstrating how quickly legal status can become irrelevant once a person is marked as an outsider.  The issue, it seems, is no longer legality. The issue is belonging.


When I was younger, I believed documents had power. Adults treated them as though they did. Passports were carefully stored. Permits were renewed. Birth certificates were tucked away in drawers and folders. Documents opened doors, crossed borders and settled questions. Or so I thought. As I grew older, I realised that documents answer only certain kinds of questions. They can tell people where you were born. They can confirm your legal status. They can prove that you are permitted to be somewhere. What they cannot do is convince someone that you belong. That lesson reveals itself in small moments: a question asked with just enough suspicion to make you uncomfortable, a joke that everyone else laughs at, the pause that follows your …

author: WoMin
title: On Language and the Pedagogy of Liberation
content:
Across Africa, colonialism was not only a project of economic exploitation and political domination; it was also a project of language and cultural control. Colonial rule sought to determine not only who governed and who had access to resources but also elevated European languages as symbols of intelligence and authority, while African languages were systematically marginalised. 


African literature captured this contradiction. In

So Long a Letter

, Mariama Bâ writes from within the tensions of expressing African women’s realities through a language inherited from colonial rule. Ama Ata Aidoo’s novel

Our Sister Killjoy

, similarly, exposes the uneasy relationship between English as a language of literary expression and also as a reminder of cultural displacement. These reflections continue to resonate with present-day realities across the continent, where language remains deeply entangled with questions of power, culture, identity, class, gender, and belonging.  


Today, access to education, legal systems, government services, and political participation in many African countries still depends heavily on competence in colonial languages such as English, French, or Portuguese.  


In Nigeria, for example, although more than 250 languages are spoken across the country, English remains the dominant language of governance, education or even policy discourse. Similar dynamics persist elsewhere on the continent. In Tanzania, although Kiswahili is the national language, many court judgments continue to be delivered in English. Citizens who do not understand English must depend on interpreters to comprehend legal decisions affecting their lives. 


For peasant and working-class women confronting mining, oil extraction, logging, large-scale agricultural investments, and other extractive projects, language exclusions carry profound consequences especially for rural women whose language is deeply tied to their relationship to land, water, forests, food systems, ancestry, and survival.  


Where information about government-proposed projects is often delivered in foreign languages without clarifying their implications including the terms of the proposed project, the risks it poses, the compensation being offered, or the legal mechanisms available to challenge it, their ability to give meaningful consent or organise resistance against it, then language becomes a question of power. 


Language in Women Learning Liberation and Translation as a Tool of Resistance

 


Language was central to the development of

Women Learning Liberation

  (WLL), WoMin’s 18-month political education course for frontline women activists. The first WLL cohort began in July 2024, bringing together 60 women from Cameroon, Guinea Conakry, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, South Africa, and Uganda. From the beginning, WLL understood political education not as the transfer of knowledge from experts to communities, but as a process of collective learning rooted in women’s own experiences and struggles. 


The Ugandan WLL cohort spoke eight languages and represented five different community struggles. English could provide a common language for some discussions, but relying exclusively on it would have risked excluding women from fully expressing their experiences, questions, analysis, and political imagination. WLL therefore deliberately incorporated interpretation into the political education process. Facilitation moved between English, Luganda, Runyoro, and Kinyarwanda, while participants themselves became active in ensuring that interpretation was taking place. 


As

Ugandan facilitator Sostine Namanya

 explained: “Language can work, but language needs to be budgeted for, language needs to be prepped for.” 


In many African contexts, people come from diverse language backgrounds and often speak multiple languages. While English or French may serve as common languages, reliance on colonial languages can reproduce unequal power relations and weaken movements. Interpretation and translation therefore become powerful tools for building multilingual and robust movements capable of deepening collective participation.  


In 2024, WoMin launched materials supporting the

Right To Say NO  campaign in East Africa

 in five languages, which join a plethora of knowledge materials and resources such as its award-winning film,

Women Hold up the Sky

 (2021) and a comic book,

Voices against Extractivism: Sheroes for Change

. The act of interpretation and …

author: Akal Mohan
title: The Quiet Struggle of a Non-Practicing Christian
content:
“Between religion and my black skin there shall be a sky’s distance until the day I hear the call to atonement.”-Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor, The Dragonfly Sea


I feel like a fraud writing about religion. I feel so because I am an African who was Christian, yet I know very little about African Christianity. My (initial) faith was mostly informed by Western Christianity. It was embedded in the Seventh Day Adventist Church. I was born into, schooled in, and had lived by the Adventist teachings for most of my life. It is a denomination I am still indoctrinated by. If you know nothing about the Adventist Church, here is what you should know: It is a faith that is to date rooted in doctrines that have remained static over the years. Their command and church manual is universal and whereas context and culture should be considered in every religious practice, the Adventist Church regards them as inapt. Their global governing body is known as the General Conference and has its offices in Maryland, United States. This General Conference, you should know, has never had a black president since it was founded in 1863. To its staunch members, questioning the doctrines is perceived to be pillorying the church. The ultimate consequence of this is excommunication.


I give this background as a backdrop to why I am never confident writing about religion. Frankly, I have very little stake in what happens in the Church. I left Christianity half a decade ago and I have identified as agnostic ever since. I am agnostic, not atheist, because I understand that religiosity is a spiritual reality I cannot escape. “We are all religious beings,” Kenyan writer, philosopher and theologian Joe Kobuthi

says

. Joe proceeds to explain that the questions of life and meaning – existential questions – are all theological questions. I agree with Joe. My life, as I continue to experience it, is theology. My consciousness and temperament are grounded in biblical teachings. Much of the gospel is inductive to my life.


My quandary with religion and faith and belief continues to cause a disquiet in my spiritual life. The closest I can come to explaining this internal crisis is by using the words of Mahatma Gandhi in his work, “The Missionary and the Mission” where he states: “I am becoming humble enough to say that I cannot adequately represent the religion I practise by speech and pen. Language is a limitation of the truth which cannot only be represented by life.”  Gandhi’s disconcert might be limited to language and truth; my prejudice as an African extends further. Further because of the infusion of imperialism and colonization in the theology that has been passed down to me. This prejudice has overarching currents. It stays with an individual, a society, a culture and has led to a shift of indigenous moral pillars in African communities, as Dr Mwikamba has argued in his

paper

 “Changing Morals in Africa”. It is a tragedy that many Africans, me leading, cannot articulate what their true theological truth is. 


Anytime I see congregants gathered, praying in piety, I am reminded of how staunch I once was. I recall how I registered for outreach, attended fellowships, went out for mission work. These ministries gave me a tribe. It always felt like we were disciples of the same body, plighted by the same agony of bringing the lost back to Christ. We went out, our hearts devoted to The Great Commission: “Go ye and make disciples of all nations.” I have not lived in that desire for the last five years. It is a desire that I have shelved in my soul as I try to figure out what theology is practical in my reality. “Something repels the heart deeply in most organized forms of religion,” observes South African writer Bessie Head. This has been my struggle with organized religion: Its near cultic grip repels my heart. I am also occupied by the dilemmas of how to translate The Great Commission into my daily life. “We are too focused on heaven that our faith has no earthly relevance,” a pastor once said.   


***


The late Kenyan bishop and theologian Henry Okullu, in his essay, “Church and State”, opens by stating that, “One of the great issues in East Africa on which there is much confusion concerns the relationship which exists, or which should exist, between Church and State.”  Bishop Okullu, who championed pluralistic democracy and human rights, continues to write that every time the issue of the Church and State emerges, both politicians and Christians are …

author: Amelia Schafer
title: 3 National Archives Locations Are Set to Close. Tribal Docs’ Fate Is Unclear.
content:
Indigenous leaders say the US government’s decision to close the sites was made without tribal consultation.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Milwaukee, Wisconsin – The Chicago National Archives holds hundreds of thousands of Bureau of Indian Affairs records spanning nearly two centuries, but the site is set to close by the end of September.

There is no clear answer about where the documents are going or when they’ll next be accessible.

Once the site closes, it could take roughly two years for the documents to be made available again to tribal leaders, historic preservation officers and even the general public, according to an inter-agency email discussing the closure that was leaked to several news outlets at the end of June.

Documents stored at the National Archives can be crucial when it comes to assessing tribal enrollment rolls, accessing documentation of Indian trust funds and even uncovering information about the Federal Indian Boarding School era. There are maps, photos, court records, first-hand testimonies, Indigenous language materials, genealogies and more stored in the archives, all of which is at risk, according to tribal historians.

“It was never broadcasted to tribal governments, in fact, I’m not even sure there’s been a real public release of information,” Michael LaRonge, tribal historic preservation officer for the Sokagaon Band of Chippewa Indians in northern Wisconsin, told ICT.

LaRonge and others said they’d heard reports of the Chicago location closing at the end of September.

According to the leaked inter-agency email, San Francisco and Seattle’s National Archives are both slated to close as well.

“Something irreplaceable is at risk,” said Heather Hostler, a citizen of the Hoopa Valley Tribe and the executive director of California Indian Legal Services during a press conference on August 24 in San Francisco. “They are not the only way we know our history, but they are an important part of it, helping us to document the experiences of our ancestors and our sacred relationship with the United States. These records are priceless.”

Hostler said there is no clear information detailing where the records will end up.

“Decisions appear to be moving forward without meaningful tribal consultation and without a complete public understanding of what is at stake,” Hostler said during the press conference. “The United States has a trust responsibility to tribes and a duty to consult them in making decisions like the San Bruno closure. We know too well what happens when things are taken from Native people.”

Tribal Historical Preservation officers like LaRonge said they were left completely in the dark about the San Francisco site’s closure, a violation of the nation-to-nation relationship between the federal government and tribes.

Per the Administrative Procedure Act, public agencies must submit written notice to the public of their intentions in detail and allow for a public comment period. No such notice has occurred.

The National Archives has yet to issue a statement on the closures and did not respond to multiple requests for comment from ICT.

“Tribal consultation is supposed to kick in whenever there’s an effect on a tribal nation’s ability to govern themselves,” LaRonge said. “The materials there, there’s census records used by tribal enrollment offices, historical information. … there’s a host of other things [like] legal references to major Indigenous law cases all stored there. It’s kind of this odd pervasive problem.”

LaRonge said he and others from the Sokagoan community have been able to save up to travel to Chicago once a year for three years to access their records. As a result of those trips, the group has scanned copies of about 16,342 pages, LaRonge said.

It would be impossible to scan all relevant records prior to the archive’s closing. Records from the Lac Du Flambeau agency alone, which contains documents from other tribes such as Lac Du Flambeau and Red Cliff, contains over 300 linear feet of records, LaRonge said. None of those records are organized.

“We obviously don’t need all 300 linear feet, but we have to essentially go in person and search through those records because they’re not, they’re not really organized,” LaRonge said. “There’s no quick way to get through any of that archive material except to go and really kind of root through page by page.”

author: Daron Letts
title: Researchers study oil-eating microbes off Hudson Bay coast
content:
A team of Inuit and southern researchers is using the water off Chesterfield Inlet as a living laboratory as they study naturally occurring microbes that feed on oil residue in the ocean.


Run out of the Centre for Observation Science at the University of Manitoba, in Winnipeg, since 2022, the Genice II project blends scientific method with Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit, or traditional Inuit knowledge. It builds on data from previous studies in Winnipeg and at the University of Calgary in 2015 and 2020.


The researchers are looking for microbial communities beneath the ice. These samples form baseline data with which subsequent samples may be compared, to identify any population changes, Collins said.


Microbes are the foundation of the marine food chain, ultimately supporting the species that make up country food.


Microbial activity is key for kiviaq (fermented seabirds) and mikigaq (fermented whale), by supplying the nutrients and vitamins necessary for fermentation.


Microbes can be harmful, in the form of algae blooms, which can choke out other aquatic life. These varieties are not evident in the region, Collins said.


The microbes pertinent to Genice II naturally maintain water quality in marine and freshwater environments by degrading and decontaminating human pollutants, which can include fossil fuels, the researchers have found. They can monitor these microbes to detect oil spills.


So far, researchers have not detected any disturbances that would indicate an oil spill occurred.


“If there were a spill, we would see indicator species that eat the oil,” Collins said.


A recent 50-litre

oil spill

 300 kilometres upstream, near Baker Lake, is not expected to affect findings, Collins added.


However, with increased shipping through the region, the risk of spills is ever present.


Chesterfield Inlet narrowly

escaped environmental calamity

 in 2012 when the MV Nanny ran aground in the inlet carrying almost 3 million litres of oil.


The research reveals that the microbes behave differently in the North than they do in warmer climes, due to the low ocean temperature, Collins said.


It takes Arctic microbes one month to begin eating the same amount of oil that microbes in the Gulf of Mexico begin eating after two weeks, he said.


The scientists work with the Sapujiyiit Society, a grassroots group of Inuit knowledge-keepers that provides community-led environmental monitoring in the hamlet. They collect samples on the ice.


“That relationship has been very important to make our project work,” said microbiologist Eric Collins.


Some new microbial species have also been discovered along the way. Inuit of all ages will be asked to come up with Inuktitut names for these species in October, said Nicole Wilson, associate professor of environment and geography at the University of Manitoba.

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Community mourns Joan Phillip, Amshen, who fought for justice and ‘loved very hard’
content:
Joan Phillip, Amshen, stands next to the Grandview Park Cenotaph in 2024. She passed away on Aug. 28, 2026, at the age of 74.

Photo by Kayla MacInnis


Fearless. Fierce. Wise. Courageous. Cherished.


Those were just a few of the words that colleagues and loved ones used to describe the late Joan Phillip, Amshen, at her funeral service in snpink’tn (Penticton, B.C.) on Wednesday. 


Before Amshen was laid to rest in the community cemetery in syilx Okanagan homelands, leaders, dignitaries, and people from near and far packed the Outma Sqilx’W Cultural School’s gym — with hundreds more watching a livestream online — to remember the beloved leader.


“It was one of the dreams and hopes of our people for years to have our own school in our community to teach our children. Joan helped get this here,” said caxasket Joseph Pierre of the Penticton Indian Band (PIB), who moderated the funeral service.


Amshen,

an Indigenous leader and lifelong activist from the Tsleil-Waututh Nation

, died last Friday on Aug. 28, at the age of 74. Her grandfather was the late Chief Dan George.


At the time of her death, she was serving as a member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) of British Columbia. She represented the Vancouver-Strathcona riding — previously Vancouver-Mount Pleasant — through the NDP, a position she held since 2023.


‘Do not be afraid to stand like Joan stood’


Amshen spent more than 20 years as the lands administrator for PIB, retiring from that role in 2019. She was a member of the Penticton Band Council and married to Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, the president of the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs, who was chief of PIB for 14 years. The couple split their time between “Vancouver” and snpink’tn.


“I thank the Creator, I thank kʷuləncutn, for putting Joan on my path — for herself and my path,” the Grand Chief said at Amshen’s funeral, whom he had grown to know as “Bunny” during their marriage.


“We were able to have such a wonderful life together.  I feel no regrets. My heart is in a good place. I feel gratitude. I feel amazing, powerful gratitude, that I had the opportunity to be together with Joan. To share her life, to share her love, to share her principles and integrity.”


A staunch advocate for Indigenous title and rights; the wellbeing of the land and for future generations, Amshen’s relatives recalled a woman “who had no fear” and “stood up” against colonial injustices.


“Joan was all about children, young people, our Elders. People in the Downtown Eastside absolutely loved Joan, because they knew she was there for them,” said the Grand Chief.


People shared stories of her involvement with the Red Power Movement and the Native Alliance for Red Power when she was just 16 years old, as well as her moments of solidarity with the Oka Crisis, the Gustafsen Lake standoff, and Standing Rock.


In one of her final acts in the fight for the rights of Indigenous Peoples, Amshen stood up against B.C. Premier David Eby and her own political party earlier this year, when attempts were made to amend the province’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA).


“I was so proud of her,” Phillip said of his late wife and her opposition to amend DRIPA.


“We’re not oil people in this room. We’re not pipeline people. We’re not corporate people. We’re Indians. That was the beauty of Joan — she knew that. She knew which team she was on, and why she was on that team.”


While they mourned her loss, the Grand Chief and others in Amshen’s close circle encouraged people in the room to honour her legacy by continuing on with the work that she had committed her life to.


“When we move forward in the work that’s ahead of us, do not be afraid to stand like Joan stood,” said the Grand Chief.


“Don’t be afraid to stand up. Joan’s principle was: we have to stand up, no matter what. So I ask you to do that.”


Stewart and Joan Phillip stand with their fists in the air against Kinder Morgan on Burnaby Mountain.

 File photo


‘That legacy needs to carry on’


Eby was in attendance for Amshen’s funeral, and was the first guest invited to speak at her service. While acknowledging that it was a difficult day for everyone in the room, he described his colleague as “a remarkable person with such incredible history in our province.”


“Joan was absolutely fearless. She’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. And she was an incredible friend and colleague,” said Eby.
