title: Ağız sağlığında sessiz tehlike: Göz ardı edilmemesi gereken 5 diş belirtisi
content:
Ağız ve diş sağlığı, genel vücut sağlığının en önemli göstergelerinden biri. Dünya Sağlık Örgütü (WHO) verilerine göre, tedavi edilmeyen ağız rahatsızlıkları sistemik enfeksiyonlar, kalp-damar hastalıkları ve diyabet kontrolsüzlüğü gibi ciddi sağlık sorunlarına zemin hazırlayabiliyor. İşte, Diş Hekimliği Araştırmaları Uluslararası Derneği (IADR) verileri ve klinik değerlendirmelere dayanarak belirlenen, “geçer” denilerek ihmal edilmemesi gereken 5 kritik belirti...

Diş eti kanaması, toplumda en sık karşılaşılan ancak "sert fırçalamadandır" denilerek en çok ihmal edilen semptomların başında gelir. Klinik araştırmalar, sağlıklı bir diş etinin basınç altında dahi kanamaması gerektiğini gösterir. Kanama, diş eti iltihabı aşamasının en belirgin göstergesidir. Müdahale edilmediğinde, dişleri tutan kemik dokusunun kaybına yol açan periodontitis tablosuna ilerleyebilir.

Sadece sıcak ya da soğuk gıdalarla değil, besinleri çiğnerken veya dişi dişe bastırırken hissedilen ani ve keskin ağrı, genellikle yapıyla ilgili bir hasara işaret eder. Bu belirti; derin bir çürüğün diş sinirine ulaştığını, dişte mikroskobik bir çatlak oluştuğunu ya da kök ucunda iltihabi bir lezyon geliştiğini gösterir. Çatlak diş sendromu ve kök ucu enfeksiyonları erken müdahale edilmediğinde diş kaybıyla sonuçlanabilir.

Sabahları oluşan geçici ağız kokusunun aksine, fırçalama ve gargara kullanımına rağmen geçmeyen kronik ağız kokusu bir hijyen eksikliğinden ziyade tıbbi bir belirtidir. Periodontal ceplerde biriken anaerobik bakterilerin ürettiği sülfür bileşikleri bu duruma neden olur. Araştırmalar, kronik halitosis vakalarının yüzde 85’ten fazlasının gizli diş eti hastalıkları, diş taşları ve dolguların altındaki ikincil çürüklerden kaynaklandığını ortaya koyuyor.

Dişlerin normalden daha uzun görünmesi, diş etlerinin çekilerek kök yüzeylerinin açığa çıktığını gösterir. Kök yüzeyini kaplayan sement dokusu, mine tabakası kadar sert olmadığı için aşınmaya ve çürümeye karşı son derece hassastır. Diş eti çekilmesi; bakteriyel plak birikimi, yanlış fırçalama tekniği veya diş sıkma gibi nedenlerle gelişir ve zamanla diş destek dokularının kaybına yol açar.

Soğuk bir içecek veya sıcak bir çorba tüketildiğinde yaşanan ve saniyeler içinde geçen anlık sızlamalar genellikle hafif mine aşınmalarına işaret eder. Ancak hassasiyet saniyelerce sürüyor, zonklamaya dönüşüyor ve uyarandan bağımsız olarak devam ediyorsa, dişin pulpa dokusunda geri dönüşümsüz bir iltihaplanma başlamış demektir. Bu durum, kanal tedavisi gerektiren klinik bir tablodur.

title: "Le socialisme sauvage", chapitre 2
content:
Deuxiéme extrait du livre : "Le socialisme sauvage : essai sur l'auto-organisation et la démocratie directe dans les luttes de 1789 à nos jours"


à l'heure où la sociale-démocratie reprend du galon, sous ses divers avatars réformistes et léninistes, menaçant de récupérer les luttes à venir


Nous reproduisons ici en brochures les différents chapitres du livre « le socialisme sauvage », de Charles Reeve. Il retrace l'histoire de diverses luttes depuis la Révolution Française, via un axe anarchiste, communiste antiautoritaire, ultragauchiste, autonome, etc..


Son but est de relire l'histoire révolutionnaire non depuis l'angle traditionnel et confus de « la révolution contre les bourgeois/les aristocrates » - qui fait comme si la révolution était un bloc - mais depuis un axe fondamental souvent oublié : celui des divers courants libertaires contre les tendances autoritaires du socialisme.


On regrettera certains défauts importants, qu'il est bon d'avoir en tête en parcourant le bouquin. Notamment le fait que les luttes abordées sont très majoritairement des luttes blanches. Ou que l'angle pris fait souvent la part belle aux figures et organisations militantes officielles - là où il serait intéressant de se concentrer un peu plus sur l'action et l'organisation directes du prolétariat.


Ces points étant dits, ce livre apporte de nombreuses informations historiques importantes, souvent effacées de l'histoire des luttes. Il permet ainsi, de façon méthodique et détaillée, de remettre plusieurs points sur les i concernant la question de l'autoritarisme. C'est une chose qui nous semble plus qu'utile à l'heure où la sociale-démocratie reprend du galon, sous ses divers avatars réformistes et léninistes, menaçant de récupérer les luttes à venir.


Bonne lecture !

title: Septa (Ceuta) : L'Europe veut nous imposer une réalité qui n'est pas la notre
content:
COMMUNIQUÉ DE CADRE CAGOULE — 25/08


L'Europe veut présenter le Maroc comme un pays sûr. Un pays paisible. Un pays stable. Un pays vers lequel on pourrait renvoyer des personnes sans même leur demander pourquoi elles l'ont fui.


Mais à Ceuta, nous avons vu une autre réalité.


 Depuis le 30 juillet, des milliers de Marocaines et de Marocains sont entrés à Ceuta. Pendant plus de vingt jours, nos frères et sœurs harragas ont affronté la faim, les chasses à l'homme, les coups, les humiliations ainsi que les violences physiques et psychologiques. De la part de la police, de la Guardia Civil, de l'armée, des fascistes de Ceuta et de l'État. Et malgré tout, les harragas ont résisté. Parce qu'ils savent mieux que quiconque ce qu'ils cherchent à fuir.


Le Maroc du football, de la télévision, de YouTube, de la publicité et du tourisme n'est pas le Maroc dans lequel vivent les Marocains. La réalité, c'est une fille de neuf ans qui traverse une frontière à la nage pour quitter le Maroc. La réalité, ce sont des mineurs qui quittent leur foyer et entrent dans la mer parce que l'avenir les terrifie. Des filles qui partent parce qu'elles ne sont pas en sécurité. Des mères qui traversent avec leurs enfants parce qu'elles craignent la faim et un avenir inconnu. Des jeunes femmes et des jeunes hommes qui grandissent dans un pays devenu une prison géante. Humiliation. Peur. Répression. Torture. Ignorance imposée.


Et l'Europe appelle cela : « SAFE ». La démocratie est-elle un droit pour tout le monde, ou seulement pour celles et ceux qui possèdent un passeport rouge ou une peau blanche ? Le colonialisme a-t-il pris fin ? Ou a-t-il simplement changé de visage ? L'Europe veut que la pauvreté, la faim et l'humiliation au Maroc paraissent naturelles. Comme si la pauvreté était tombée du ciel. Comme si la répression n'avait aucun auteur. Comme si des personnes avaient simplement décidé, un matin, de se jeter à la mer. L'Europe refuse de considérer la pauvreté dans son contexte politique. Parce que dès que la pauvreté devient politique, quelqu'un doit en répondre.


L'Union européenne ferme les yeux sur les crimes des dictatures africaines lorsque ses intérêts sont protégés. Dans le même temps, elle finance des frontières qui tuent, frappent, traquent et emprisonnent celles et ceux qui fuient : LA PAUVRETÉ. LA GUERRE. LE FASCISME. LA RÉPRESSION.


L'Europe protège les régimes que les personnes tentent de fuir, puis criminalise celles et ceux qui leur échappent. Au Maroc, le salaire minimum se situe autour de 3 000 dirhams. Tu travailles toute la journée. Le loyer engloutit la majeure partie de ton salaire. Pendant ce temps, des entreprises et des investissements européens profitent d'une main-d'œuvre bon marché et d'un système politique qui leur garantit un mot sacré : « STABILITÉ ».


La stabilité pour le capital. Le silence pour tous les autres. L'Union européenne ignore-t-elle réellement la situation sociale au Maroc ? Ignore-t-elle ce que les personnes gagnent, le prix des loyers et le coût de la survie ? Ses analystes sont-ils véritablement aussi incompétents ? Ou l'Europe sait-elle exactement ce qui se passe ? Peut-être que la dictature ne devient un problème que lorsqu'elle cesse de servir les intérêts européens.


Le colonialisme n'est pas seulement un drapeau planté sur une terre. Le colonialisme, c'est aussi : Qui décide de la valeur de ton travail. Qui profite de ta pauvreté. Qui arme les frontières qui te maintiennent enfermé. Qui décide des endroits où ton corps a le droit de se déplacer. Qui attend de toi que tu travailles pour presque rien et que tu meures en silence si tu refuses.


Les harragas ne sont pas une main-d'œuvre bon marché attendant d'être exploitée. Ce sont des travailleuses et des travailleurs libres. Ils revendiquent le droit de travailler dans la dignité. Le droit de vivre dans la dignité. Travailler douze heures par jour pour 300 euros par mois, pendant que 200 euros disparaissent dans le loyer, ce n'est pas la dignité. Il faut appeler cela par son nom : de l'esclavage économique.


À Ceuta, les harragas ne demandaient pas de nourriture. Leur slogan dans les rues était clair :


« ASILO, ASILO, NO COMIDA. »


L'ASILE. PAS LA NOURRITURE.


Parce que nous savons partager la nourriture. Nous venons d'Afrique. Même lorsque la vie est difficile, nous apprenons à partager entre nous le peu que nous possédons. Ils ne demandaient pas à l'Europe de les nourrir. Ils exigeaient que l'Europe cesse de leur refuser le …

author: Megan Rose
title: Trump Admin Blocked Prosecution of ICE Agent for Minneapolis Shooting
content:
The agent allegedly shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg during Operation Metro Surge and then lied about it.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Over the “strongest possible” objections from the federal prosecutor handling the case, leaders at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., quashed plans to bring civil rights charges against an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent accused of shooting a Venezuelan immigrant and then lying about it.

The agent, 52-year-old Christian Castro, allegedly shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg in Minneapolis this January during Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration’s immigration blitz that sent thousands of federal agents into the state. The incident was one of three shootings by immigration agents in the city, the other two of which were fatal.

Federal prosecutors in Minnesota had been preparing to charge Castro with deprivation of rights under color of law for the shooting of Sosa-Celis, according to several people familiar with the case. Those charges are similar to the ones leveled against Minneapolis police officers accused in George Floyd’s killing and can carry hefty prison sentences.

Late on Tuesday, Matthew Evans, the assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota in charge of the case, told lawyers for Sosa-Celis and other victims to prepare for Castro to be charged “only with False Statements,” according to an email that was reviewed by ProPublica.

That charge would likely carry a far less severe punishment if he were convicted.

“This is being directed by the Main Justice and the US Attorney,” Evans wrote in a remarkably candid account of internal deliberations. “I objected in the strongest possible terms and fought it as hard as I could. It wasn’t enough.”

He wrote that the false statement charges could come soon and would likely be filed under seal.

“It has been an honor and a privilege to try to get justice for your clients,” Evans concluded the email.

A DOJ official said civil rights charges require consultation with the civil rights division in Washington, and “any charging decisions that come out of such investigations are collaborative and deliberative and adhere to the facts and law of that specific case and controversy.”

The agency “has not yet reached a conclusion on this matter and will never rush an investigative process and the thorough review of all evidence,” the official said.

Evans and a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota declined to comment. An attorney for Sosa-Celis did not return phone calls from a reporter. Castro, who has an outstanding warrant in Minnesota for this case, could not be reached for comment.

Under the Trump administration, the Justice Department’s civil rights division has been thinned and has dropped some Biden-era oversight of law enforcement agencies. This move by the DOJ is likely to fuel further concerns that the department is operating more in support of President Donald Trump’s political agenda than to preserve the rule of law. Earlier this year, a ProPublica analysis found that in almost every instance of immigration agents shooting people, Trump’s administration blamed the injured and dead within hours of the incident. In many of those cases, federal or local police declined to investigate the agents.

Castro, who was put on leave by the Department of Homeland Security, is also facing multiple state felony charges in Minnesota, including assault with a dangerous weapon. After he left Minneapolis and returned to Texas, Minnesota officials had requested state officials there extradite Castro to face the charges, but Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to cooperate. Castro had been held for 90 days in jail while the two states fought over the extradition. He was released last week.

Sosa-Celis was shot on Jan. 14, as Castro and another ICE agent chased Alfredo Aljorna, an immigrant from Venezuela, after a traffic stop. Aljorna ran to his home, which he shared with Sosa-Celis. The two men made it inside after a brief scramble, and Castro fired through the closed door, “knowing [the home] was occupied by several people,” according to state charging documents. One witness said there were two children in the house when Castro shot into it. Sosa-Celis was hit in the leg.

ICE agents then deployed tear gas into the home and took the men and their partners into custody, according to the documents and other court …

author: Brad Reed
title: Republicans Panic as Gas Prices Hit Another Record High Ahead of Midterms
content:
Republicans’ own internal polling reportedly shows voters blame the price hikes on Trump’s war on Iran.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The price of diesel fuel in the US hit another record high on Saturday, as data published by the American Automobile Association showed the average cost for a gallon of diesel now stands at $5.88.

According to a Saturday report from Axios, incumbent Republicans are fretting about the impact that skyrocketing gasoline and diesel prices will have on the 2026 midterm elections, particularly since their own internal polling shows voters are placing blame for the price hikes on President Donald Trump’s illegal war with Iran.

“Diesel’s at an all-time high,” one GOP operative told Axios. “Gas is about $4 a gallon. We can’t message that away.”

Another Republican source told Axios that GOP candidates don’t even have the option of distancing themselves from the president and his unpopular war given the iron grip he has on voters they will need to turn out in crucial races.

“We have no choice,” said the source. “We’re stuck on the boat with him whether we like it or not.”

US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy tried to spin the record-high diesel prices as something outside the president’s control during a Saturday interview on Fox News.

“When you look at diesel, you have to look at Russia and Ukraine,” Duffy said. “Russia was a major exporter, the second-biggest exporter in the world, on diesel. They stopped their exports, so that puts pressure on the global market. But President Trump has pushed American energy dominance, we are producing more energy now than in the past.”

Duffy added that “it’s only President Trump who’s trying to drive these prices down,” even though the president’s war has been the primary reason they’ve been going up.

Fox & Friends weekend host Charlie Hurt gives Trump credit for record high diesel prices: "Uhhh, they'd be a lot higher if it wasn't for the efforts of the administration" "When you look at diesel, you have to look at Russia and Ukraine," Duffy replies 🥴 pic.twitter.com/Wm5bLJ6exA

As a report published Friday by The Associated Press explained, the cost of diesel has a particularly strong impact on the price of food since the fuel is used to power both farm equipment and the trucks used to deliver food to grocery stores.

“Fuel accounts for roughly 15% to 30% of the total cost of food, according to the Independent Grocers Alliance, a grouping of 7,500 global supermarkets,” reported the AP. “So higher diesel costs often result in more expensive groceries, although it can take a while for energy shocks to wind their way through the supply chain.”

The rising cost of groceries has been a major source of stress for US consumers for years, and Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign vowed that prices on groceries would come down starting on his very first day in office.

author: Alaa Serhal
title: Palestinian Refugees in Lebanon Struggle to Survive as UNRWA Cuts Essential Aid
content:
US and Israeli attacks on the agency have caused severe budget shortfalls, leading to aid cuts at six refugee camps.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In the streets of Nahr al-Bared camp in northern Lebanon, where alleyways are barely wide enough to walk through, and buildings crowd out the sky, 45-year-old Palestinian refugee Aziza Wahbeh measures the long hours of another day.

There is the electricity that comes for only two hours a day, the water families must buy because none is supplied, the rising rent for cramped and aging homes, and the lack of work that has left many young people unable to support their families.

Wahbeh, who lives with a chronic kidney stone, says every month forces her family to choose between food and medicine — a situation facing almost a thousand other families here.

She is one of tens of thousands of Palestinian residents across Lebanon’s 12 refugee camps who have long relied on the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) for food, schooling, healthcare, and employment. Excluded by law from Lebanon’s economy, the majority of roughly 300,000 Palestinian refugees in Lebanon have no safety net beyond the agency.

But now, facing its worst financial crisis since its founding in 1949, UNRWA is making choices between which camps to support and which to leave without necessary aid. The last emergency cash assistance Wahbeh received from UNRWA was distributed in the spring.

Then, in May, the agency made the decision to exclude six camps from its emergency cash assistance program on the grounds that they were not “directly affected” by the ongoing conflict in Lebanon: Nahr al-Bared and Baddawi in the north, Ein al-Hilweh and Mieh Mieh in the Saida area, and Mar Elias and Dbayeh in Beirut.

The decision, impacting thousands of families, triggered immediate protest. In mid-June, Palestinian factions and popular committees held simultaneous sit-ins outside the agency’s offices in Nahr al-Bared and Baddawi, calling the distribution unjust and demanding criteria that applied to all refugees regardless of area.

The grievance has since widened. Demonstrations broke out in Beirut on August 14 against cuts to UNRWA services, demanding monthly cash assistance for every Palestinian family without exception.

Residents argue that a war which paralyzed Lebanon’s economy, drove up prices, and halted work spared no corner of the country, least of all the camps whose fragile economies depended on the Lebanese cities around them.

“We now choose between a loaf of bread and our medicine,” Wahbeh told Mondoweiss at her home in the camp. “UNRWA was the only artery sustaining us with some food assistance, medical care, and schooling for our children. For them to come now and cut the aid, and leave us out of the latest distributions, we felt we had been abandoned by the side of the road.”

Her household now runs on what her father can forage. “He goes up the mountain to gather sage and sell it,” she said. “A bunch goes for a hundred thousand lira (~1.1 cents), and that is what covers the house. If he sells, we eat for a day. If he doesn’t sell, we don’t eat.”

The decision lands at the moment of UNRWA’s deepest institutional crisis.

The crisis has its roots in early 2024, when Israel accused a number of UNRWA staff of involvement in the October 7 attacks. More than a dozen donors, led by the United States, suspended funding. Although most later resumed contributions, the damage was lasting.

The agency received $829 million in 2025, barely a quarter of its assessed needs, and faces a $100 million cash-flow deficit for 2026. A pledging conference in New York on June 30 raised only $4 million. The agency’s acting Commissioner-General, Christian Saunders, told donors on June 30 that the agency’s financial situation is unsustainable.

A succession of fragile ceasefires between Hezbollah and Israel since November 2024 has done little to ease conditions on the ground. Consumer prices rose by about 15 percent in 2025, even as annual inflation slowed from the triple-digit rates of recent years. Rents have climbed sharply as war damage, delayed reconstruction, and mass displacement compressed an already scarce housing market. The World Bank estimates the conflict caused $14 billion in economic losses and left Lebanon needing $11 billion for recovery and reconstruction.

title: 34th International Kurdish Culture Festival ends with message of “unity among Kurds”
content:
Following Abdullah Öcalan’s message, the 34th International Kurdish Culture Festival continued with speeches alongside cultural and artistic events, with slogans of “There can be no peace without a leader” rising from the crowd. Kurds from Kurdistan and their friends gathered at the festival grounds, continuing the festive atmosphere with music and traditional halay dances, while speeches from the stage emphasized the importance of preserving the Kurdish people’s language, culture, and identity. The festival’s music program continued with performances by Nahîde and Rizgar Hewramanî, while TEV-ÇAND artist Hekîm Sefkan also addressed the festival audience.


We kept our culture alive for 34 years


Drawing attention to the fact that the International Kurdish Culture Festival has continued uninterrupted for 34 years, Sefkan said the festival should not be viewed merely as a cultural and artistic event. Sefkan added that for 34 years they have gathered in the same venues to keep Kurdish culture alive, emphasizing the importance of efforts in Europe to preserve the Kurdish language and culture.


Sefkan said: “For 34 years, we have been working together in these places to keep our culture alive. We have always worked to preserve our language and culture here, in Europe. This festival is not merely a cultural and artistic event; it is also an expression of the national struggle.”


Drawing attention to the significance of the festival in the struggle to preserve the Kurdish people’s identity and sense of belonging, Sefkan said that one of the fundamental aims of the Martyrs of the Kurdistan Freedom Movement was to protect the Kurdish people’s language, culture, and identity. Emphasizing that the values created by the martyrs must be kept alive, Sefkan said: “The struggle of our martyrs, their purpose in life, was to protect our language, culture, identity, and sense of belonging. We salute their martyrdom. We once again reiterate that we will keep alive the values they created and continue along the path of their struggle.”


Sefkan added that the culture of Kurdistan should not be viewed as being limited solely to the values of the Kurdish people, adding that they also embrace the cultural and artistic values of the different peoples living in Kurdistan. Stating that the cultures of Arab, Assyrian, and Turkmen peoples are also regarded as values of Kurdistan, Sefkan continued: “We have valued our culture as well as the art and values of the other peoples of Kurdistan—the Arabs, Assyrians, and Turkmen. We have regarded them as values of Kurdistan. It has always been this way, and it will remain this way. We have always prioritized all the values and all the peoples of Kurdistan.”


Sefkan underlined that the individuals whose deaths as martyrs have been announced recently also lost their lives for this struggle and these values, stating that the martyrs’ struggle was connected to preserving the freedom, culture, and identity of the Kurdish people. “Their martyrdoms have been announced and made public recently,” Sefkan said, emphasizing that the martyrs’ struggle and aspirations were connected to the freedom of the people. “They struggled to protect our culture and identity. We owe them a debt. That is why we say once again: Martyrs never die.”

Une décision qui s'inscrit dans la continuité de la politique de l'administration Trump, qui avait déjà désigné Antifa comme organisation terroriste en 2025. L'invention de cette prétendue organisation est un stratagème visant à créer un ennemi intérieur, afin de délégitimer la dissidence et de criminaliser l'antifascisme.


Dans ce contexte, A/I est également visé, en tant que nœud technologique utilisé par les réseaux antifascistes, qui offre des outils d'autodéfense numérique et de libre communication. Outre A/I, Palestine Action et Masar Badil ont également été visés.


Il ne s'agit pas d'un épisode isolé. Du procès de Budapest aux poursuites contre les antifascistes, en passant par les recours au mandat d'arrêt européen et la fermeture de certains comptes bancaires de la caisse de solidarité Rote Hilfe, nous observons différents dispositifs qui produisent le même effet : délégitimer l'antifascisme et criminaliser la dissidence.


Le fil rouge qui les relie est la tentative d'isoler celles et ceux qui luttent, de s'attaquer aux outils d'organisation et de briser les liens de solidarité.


C'est pourquoi le soutien et la défense d'Autistici/Inventati nous concernent toutes et tous. Défendre les espaces autonomes de communication et de dissidence, c'est défendre la possibilité de construire la solidarité.

author: Michael Arria
title: Boycott of Starbucks Is Still On as Workers Press for $17 Wage and Protections
content:
On the heels of their victory on silica-based powder, baristas are urging patrons to boycott until they win a contract.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The boycott of Starbucks’ multinational coffee chain is still in full swing this Labor Day weekend as Starbucks workers push to secure a new contract.

The AFL-CIO and Chicago Teachers Union have already expressed support for the boycott, which unionized Starbucks workers initiated to support their demands for a minimum hourly wage of $17, improved staffing, and better workplace protections.

“At a time when working-class people across the country are struggling in a challenging economy, it is no longer possible to be both a Starbucks customer and in support of workers,” said Starbucks Workers United in a statement. “Choosing to spend money at Starbucks is choosing a law-breaking corporation over the baristas who make your coffee every day exactly as you ask for it.”

Starbucks Workers United was started in 2021, after the Elmwood store in Buffalo became the first Starbucks to unionize. Since then, it has grown to 12,000 members, and almost 700 Starbucks stores have been unionized. In 2025, the union won 125 elections and had an election win rate of 82 percent.

The latest boycott campaign comes amid setbacks at the federal level, as Trump’s National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) currently holds a Republican majority.

Last month, the NLRB ruled that a Starbucks manager didn’t violate labor law when she told an employee that workers from unionized stores might be prohibited from picking up shifts at non-union stores.

The case involved Alejandra Toscano, a barista who worked at the Seattle-area Holman Road store from February 2021 until July 2022. After the store voted to unionize, workers at a nearby non-union store informed Toscano that she wouldn’t be able to “borrow” shifts at locations that weren’t unionized.

Toscano asked her manager, Chelsea Zapata, whether this was correct. Zapata told her that that she had heard the same thing at a meeting with lawyers, but that “didn’t know exactly what was true,” and suggested she keep trying to pick up shifts.

The Workers United Labor Union International, which is affiliated with the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), filed a labor complaint over the issue and, in May 2023, an administrative law judge determined that Zapata had violated Section 8(a)(1) of the National Labor Relations Act.

However, this ruling was dismissed in August 2026 by the NLRB. The Trump appointees, Chairman James Murphy and member Scott Mayer, determined that Zapata had simply made an “equivocal comment” that could not be classified as an unlawful threat.

In his dissent, David Prouty, the only Democratic member of the board, said his colleagues were leaving out crucial context. In 2024, the board had determined that multiple Starbucks managers had made unlawful threats about shift borrowing at stores in Michigan, Minnesota, and other locations.

“Thus, at or around the same time that Zapata issued the threat (in response to a rumor Toscano heard from colleagues), the Respondent’s managers were violating the Act by, among other things, making those same threats at locations across the country,” it reads.

Meanwhile, in July, the NLRB prevented a Seattle Starbucks from unionizing when it ruled that the vote was invalid because it included two mail-in ballots. Once again, Prouty was the only member to object. In his dissent, he pointed out that nothing in the Board’s rules prohibits the use of mail-in ballots and that the union vote was held in 2022, when many people were still taking COVID-19 precautions and avoiding in-person meetings.

Biden-era NLRB wins for the union are also being undone.

In May, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, which has a Republican majority, vacated an NLRB decision finding that the company had illegally fired a barista over union activity in New York and, in June, the court overturned an NLRB ruling that found a Southern California worker was terminated for organizing.

Writing at Bloomberg Law in February, reporter Parker Purifoy pointed out that the new Trump-shaped NLRB could settle cases more readily, and impair the union’s litigation path. There are currently over 600 active unfair labor practice charges pending against Starbucks, which could end up being dismissed …

En France, la population détenue a augmenté de 139 % depuis 1980, atteignant 86 100 personnes en janvier 2026. Surpopulation, insalubrité, violences, maladies et suicides marquent le quotidien carcéral.


Malgré les condamnations répétées de la France par la justice européenne, l'État continue de construire des prisons et de durcir sa politique pénale. La prison punit, désocialise, détruit des liens et frappe en priorité les personnes les plus précaires et marginalisées.


Loin de réduire les violences, l'enfermement peut les aggraver et favoriser la récidive. Alors pourquoi continuons-nous à croire qu'il nous protège ?


Parce que l'insécurité est devenue un outil politique : on désigne des menaces, on construit des ennemis et on présente la punition comme une évidence. On transforme ainsi des problèmes sociaux en responsabilités individuelles.


Crève la taule 84 refuse cette logique. Nous ne voulons pas répondre à la haine par la cage, la matraque et l'humiliation, mais par la solidarité, l'organisation et les idées.


Nous sommes abolitionnistes parce que nous refusons la domination et la violence institutionnelle. L'abolition n'est pas un rêve : c'est la nécessité d'imaginer et de construire d'autres façons de prévenir les violences, de réparer les torts et de vivre ensemble.


La prison est inutile et néfaste.


L'insécurité imaginaire.


La révolution possible.


L'abolition nécessaire.

title: SEVEN DUCKS LIBERATED FROM A DECOY HUNTING STATION.
content:
North Italy, August.


received anonymously via email:


ENGLISH (translation):


“In Italy, the Senate has recently approved the reform of Law 157/1992.


Bill 1552 is now under discussion in the Chamber of Deputies. The hunting reform radically alters the historic Law 157/1992. The measure introduces the concept of ‘bioregulation’, redefining hunters as guardians of the environment and expanding the powers of the regions in wildlife management. The first dangerous change is, in fact, the alteration of the law’s title itself with the introduction of the notion of ‘management’ of wildlife, which aims to increase hunters’ involvement in local management bodies and recognises hunting as an ‘expression of a national tradition’ but also as a ‘sporting and physical activity’ and as a means of controlling invasive species. The overwhelming majority of Italians are opposed to this bloody and predatory activity, yet the Italian government has nevertheless decided to favour that 1 per cent of the population who take pleasure in abusing and plundering the woods for their own sadistic amusement: the hunters.Our response will always be one of animal liberation, because killing, abusing or keeping captive living beings who, like us, have a right to life is, in our view, unjust: we have therefore decided to go to one of the many fixed hunting posts used by hunters to free seven ducks who were shamefully kept in cages, awaiting use as live decoys – that is, as bait for other ducks that would then be killed by the cowardly hunter.


Instead of moving towards the abolition of hunting, Italy has chosen to increase the killing of animals, to expand the list of huntable species (including, if necessary for population control, even the wolf) and to allow hunters to manage all this, turning our lands into battlefields where the most dangerous predator always wins: the human being.


We say, and will always say, NO to the killing of any animal. Lex injusta non est lex.


THE A.L.F. IS WATCHING AND THERE IS NO PLACE TO HIDE.


A.L.F”


ITALIAN (original):


“In Italia in questi giorni e’ stata approvata dal Senato la riforma della Legge 157/1992.


Il DDL 1552 è ora in discussione alla Camera dei Deputati. La riforma della caccia modifica radicalmente la storica Legge 157/1992. Il provvedimento introduce il concetto di “bioregolazione”, ridefinendo i cacciatori come tutori dell’ambiente e ampliando le competenze delle Regioni nella gestione faunistica. La prima pericolosa novità infatti è il cambiamento del titolo della legge stessa con l’introduzione della nozione di «gestione» della fauna, che punta ad un maggiore coinvolgimento dei cacciatori negli organi territoriali di gestione e che riconosce la caccia come «espressione di una tradizione nazionale» ma anche come «attività sportiva e motoria» e come azione per il contenimento delle specie invasive. La stragrande maggioranza degli italiani è contro questa attività sanguinaria e predatoria, ma il governo italiano ha deciso ugualmente di favorire quell’ 1% di popolazione che si diverte ad abusare e saccheggiare i boschi per il proprio sadico divertimento: i cacciatori. La nostra risposta sarà sempre quella della liberazione animale perché uccidere, abusare, detenere essere viventi che hanno diritto come noi a vivere è per noi ingiusto: abbiamo deciso quindi di andare presso uno dei tanti appostamenti fissi utilizzati dai cacciatori per liberare n° 7 anatre vergognosamente detenute in gabbia in attesa di essere utilizzate come richiami vivi cioè come esche per altre anatre che sarebbero poi state uccise dal vigliacco cacciatore.


Invece di andare verso l’abolizione della caccia, l’Italia ha scelto di incrementare le uccisioni di animali, di aumentare le specie cacciabili (tra cui,se necessario per il contenimento, anche il lupo) e di permettere ai cacciatori di gestire tutto questo trasformando in campi di battaglia i nostri territori dove vince sempre il predatore più pericoloso: l’essere umano.


Noi diciamo e diremo sempre NO all’ uccisione di ogni animale. Lex injusta non est lex.


THE A.L.F. IS WATCHING AND THERE IS NOT PLACE TO HIDE.


A.L.F”

Desde mayo de 2025, las y los jubilados de Vicente López empezaron a organizar protestas en la misma sintonía que ocurren en el Congreso. Se juntan los miércoles por la tarde y tienen un pliego de demandas asociadas a sus condiciones de vida y al derecho a la protesta.


Denunciando el genocidio silencioso de los adultos mayores el pasado 20 de agosto. Foto: CITRUS

@citruspressok


Dialogamos con Liliana Russo, jubilada de esa organización, quien nos comentó cómo vienen sosteniendo la lucha: “Nosotros nos reunimos todos los miércoles en la avenida Maipú, frente a la quinta presidencial, en la esquina de Villate, a las 5 de la tarde en invierno y a las 6 de la tarde en verano. Bueno, queremos contarles que nosotros venimos haciendo esto desde hace casi un año y medio. Empezamos en mayo del año pasado, éramos 4 personas, y, bueno, ahora estamos de una manera sostenida, todos los miércoles con frío, calor, lluvia, lo que suceda, y somos más o menos 30, 40 personas de manera permanente”.


https://argentina.indymedia.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Liliana-Russo.mp4


Liliana Russo, Jubiladxs de Quinta de Olivos

@jubiladxs.quintaolivos


Denunciando el genocidio silencioso de los adultos mayores el pasado 20 de agosto. Foto: CITRUS

@citruspressok


“Además de esto, nosotros hacemos semaforazos en distintos lugares del distrito, convocando a jubilados que por ahí no están cercanos a la Quinta para que sepan lo que estamos haciendo y que puedan sumarse a esta lucha, porque no es bueno que se enfrente este gobierno desastroso en soledad”. Y también realizan semaforazos en los nueve barrios de Vicente López.


Camino a la manifestación por la Ley de Tierras. Foto: CITRUS

@citruspressok


En su gacetilla de prensa, además de invitar a participar de las medidas de fuerza, incluyen las exigencias que los impulsan a salir a la calle cada miércoles:


Medicamentos con descuentos del 100%.


Jubilaciones y pensiones acordes a la verdadera canasta de vida del adulto mayor.


Devolución del F.G.S. (Fondo de Garantía de Sustentabilidad de las Jubilaciones).


Retorno de la moratoria.


Basta de represión a los jubilados y a quienes acompañan su lucha.


En la proyección del documental “Los pueblos siempre vuelven” en la Casa de la Memoria y la Resistencia Jorge “Nono” Lizaso. Foto: CITRUS

@citruspressok


A estas demandas se le suman reclamos específicos al municipio de Vicente López: “el más rico del país, mientras que el 25% de sus habitantes son adultos mayores y cobran haberes de pobreza”.


Muestra de fotos con la Mesa Coordinadora. Foto: CITRUS

@citruspressok


Es por ello que exigen:


Una residencia geriátrica en cada localidad.


Subsidio para alquileres y/o disponer de viviendas en comodato.


Que el municipio retome el tema turismo para jubilados que dejó PAMI y lo implemente para los vecinos.


Implementar un servicio de remisería sin cargo para quienes tienen movilidad reducida.


Muestra de fotos y charla con jóvenes del programa Envión. Foto: CITRUS

@citruspressok


En nuestro intercambio con Liliana, también nos comentó que protestan los miércoles por los 30 mil desaparecidos y que el día no fue elegido al azar: “Nos faltan 30.000 jubilados, y cuando decimos esto estamos resignificando los días miércoles. Entre las actividades que realizaron en este primer año y medio de lucha, está su presencia en la Plaza de Mayo el 24 de marzo; también en la protesta por la ley de tierras y su participación en la mesa coordinadora de jubilados.

author: Ariana Figueroa
title: Trump Is Dismantling TPS Country by Country. Salvadorans Fear They’re Next.
content:
El Salvador’s Temporary Protected Status is set to expire September 9, leaving roughly 170,000 immigrants at risk.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

For years, Jose Palma has advocated for immigrants with Temporary Protected Status who hail from countries deemed too unstable for return.

But as the Trump administration has stripped those humanitarian protections for nearly a million people, the Salvadoran national is uncertain if his own legal status will remain in place next week.

“I’m going day by day,” Palma, who lives in Texas, told States Newsroom in an interview.

Within two years under the Trump administration, the bipartisan humanitarian Temporary Protected Status program created by Congress in 1990 and signed into law by former Republican President George H.W. Bush has been nearly obliterated.

Palma first obtained TPS in 2001, along with roughly 170,000 recipients from El Salvador, due to several earthquakes that displaced more than one-sixth of the population and left thousands dead. The United States renewed protections over the years, citing continued displacement and ongoing violence.

But the TPS designation for El Salvador is set to expire Sept. 9, and the Department of Homeland Security has made no indication if protections will be renewed.

Under DHS policy, an announcement typically is made 60 days in advance of the date of a TPS expiration if a renewal is planned.

Democratic Rep. Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, who helped write the statute for TPS when he was a congressional staffer, said he’s asked Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to renew protections for El Salvador.

“I still haven’t received a response back,” McGovern said during a Thursday press conference at the U.S. Capitol. He was joined by Nebraska GOP Rep. Don Bacon, who said many Salvadoran TPS recipients work and live in his Omaha district.

DHS did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment.

The Trump administration’s position on the program is that it’s “temporary,” and that country conditions have improved, despite warnings from the State Department to not travel to some of those countries where TPS designation has ended, such as Haiti.

If TPS for El Salvador ends, only 103,000 out of initially 1.3 million recipients from around the globe will have protections: 150 from Lebanon, 1,790 from Sudan and 101,150 from Ukraine.

TPS is granted to nationals who hail from a country experiencing a natural disaster, violence, or other extreme circumstances, allowing them to remain in the U.S. and obtain work permits.

Some protections can last through six-to-18-month cycles, and each renewal process requires a TPS holder to go through a background check and other vetting.

Before the second Trump administration, 17 countries were in the program. Only four, including El Salvador, remain as the White House has forged ahead aggressively on its mass deportation campaign.

The Supreme Court made the move easier after it ruled this summer that decisions from the executive branch to end TPS were not subject to judicial review. The order meant that lower courts that initially blocked the Trump administration from ending the designations had to reverse their decisions.

Now recipients face the end of TPS with just 60 days’ notice.

“It’s one of those things that is kind of cruel, to have families who are stable and have been stable for decades, to have people who have been doing everything the government asked them to do for 25 years, and suddenly, if the decision is to end TPS, provided only 60 days protection before forcing people to go back to a country they haven’t been for decades,” Palma said.

One of the first countries after TPS was written into law to receive the designation was El Salvador.

Stripping TPS from Salvadorans would not only harm the U.S. economy, but it would also negatively impact El Salvador’s fragile economy, advocates predict. More than one quarter of El Salvador’s Gross Domestic Product comes from family members sending money back to relatives in their country of origin, known as remittances.

“El Salvador’s economy has been built thanks to all the remittances,” said Ana María Méndez-Dardón, the director for Central America at the Washington Office on Latin America, or WOLA. “So if people are returning, that would have a huge impact because the economy depends on the money that …

author: Unknown
title: From Afghanistan to Kurdistan: Women resist together
content:
An event titled “Five Years of Resistance: Our Voices Remain Loud” was held in Jena, Germany on Friday to mark five years of Taliban rule in Afghanistan. The event focused on the resistance of Afghan women in Herat, Kabul, and Bamyan, their organizing efforts, and the question of how women around the world can fight together against patriarchal violence and oppression. The event was organized by Netzwerk gegen Feminizide (Network Against Femicides) Thüringen, Gemeinsam Kämpfen (Fighting Together), and Wisdom House – Free Education for Afghan Girls.


Participants watched a documentary about women’s resistance in Afghanistan. The film shows how women continue to organize, create spaces for education, and bring their protests into the public sphere despite massive repression by the Taliban. It made one point particularly clear: resistance does not begin only with the direct struggle against the Taliban. It begins earlier—at home, within families, wherever women are subjected to patriarchal violence and oppression.


Women are deprived of their rights, pushed out of public life, and continue to face severe violence. Suicides and femicides are part of a reality that persists. And while women in Afghanistan struggle for their freedom and their lives under these conditions, the German federal government cooperates with the Taliban and organizes deportations to Afghanistan.


Afterward, poems and statements by participants were read aloud, and artistic works by young women from Afghanistan were presented. Their perspectives made clear that resistance takes many forms: through art and education, organizing, public protest, and the everyday decision not to submit to patriarchal domination. The discussion that followed centered above all on one question: How can women around the world organize together to issue a collective challenge to global patriarchy?


The philosophy of “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom] played a central role in this discussion. It stands for the international networking of women’s organizations, self-organization in all areas of society, and the development of an autonomous, self-determined identity. Rather than waiting for existing social structures to grant them freedom, women should organize themselves and create their own spaces, structures, and political perspectives.


At the same time, the responsibility of men was also addressed. Many men shared the view that they often do not have enough courage to stand up against the Taliban, but also against patriarchal structures and violence within their own families. What is needed, therefore, are men who do more than simply express their solidarity—men who actively stand alongside women and challenge patriarchal relations both within themselves and together with other men.


It was also emphasized that the history of patriarchy must be understood collectively: “Patriarchy is not an immutable or natural state of affairs. It is a social order that emerged historically and can therefore also be overcome. The question is what kind of society we want to build in its place—and what role women will have within it. The values embodied by free and self-determined women must be placed at the center.”


Struggles across borders are connected


The importance of international solidarity was also highlighted by the participants, as women’s struggles take place under different conditions across the world, yet they are interconnected. Resistance should not be understood as a series of separate struggles. The revolution in Kurdistan, “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî,” the revolution in Iran and Rojhilat, the resistance of women in Abya Yala and Afghanistan, and the struggle against femicides in Germany and around the world are all part of the same struggle. The aim is to learn from one another and from different experiences and forms of organizing, to build international networks, and to make visible together that patriarchal violence is not an individual issue, but a societal and global problem.


One participant raised an important point: “Even if an event like this does not yet bring together 200 people, that does not mean the resistance is small. Every person present has consciously chosen to fight for freedom. Within that lies a spark of hope from which the next steps can emerge. It is not only about numbers, but about the significance of each individual’s courage to choose resistance anew every day.”

title: Ο πρύτανης ΕΜΠ σε ρόλο κατηγόρου, δικαστή και εκτελεστή
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης:

Ο πρύτανης ΕΜΠ σε ρόλο κατηγόρου, δικαστή και εκτελεστή


Πόσο απόλυτα ανεξέλεγκτη καθίσταται η εξουσία ενός πρύτανη, με βάση το νομικό πλαίσιο επιθετικής αποδημοκρατικοποίησης των ΑΕΙ που έχει κατασκευάσει η κυβέρνηση Μητσοτάκη;


Η καταγγελία προπτυχιακών, μεταπτυχιακών και υποψήφιων διδακτόρων του Εθνικού Μετσόβειου Πολυτεχνείου σχηματίζει μια εικόνα με διαπλεκόμενους ευνοούμενους της πρυτανικής αρχής που χρησιμοποιούνται ως «μάρτυρες» – και, μάλιστα, με ψευδείς καταθέσεις – εναντίον υποψήφιου διδάκτορα ο οποίος είχε ήδη στοχοποιηθεί προσωπικά από τον πρύτανη, Ιωάννη Χατζηγεωργίου με μήνυση του τελευταίου για τα γεγονότα της

«Βραδιάς του Ερευνητή» το 2024

.


Ακολουθεί το κείμενο της καταγγελίας:


Η πρυτανική αρχή του ΕΜΠ προχωρά στην κατασκευή πειθαρχικής δίωξης-σκευωρίας προς πολιτικά ενεργό Υποψήφιο Διδάκτορα του ΕΜΠ.


Την Δευτέρα 7/9, στις 17:00, ο υποψήφιος διδάκτορας Αρχιτεκτονικής του ΕΜΠ καλείται σε ακρόαση στο πειθαρχικό συμβούλιο για τρία διαφορετικά περιστατικά που αναφέρονται στην πολιτική του δράση τα προηγούμενα χρόνια. Το πειθαρχικό συμβούλιο θα διεξαχθεί ηλεκτρονικά και “κεκλεισμένων των θυρών”, ενώ παρότι ο υποψήφιος διδάκτορας έχει αιτηθεί αναβολή λόγω πρόσφατης αλλαγής του δικηγόρου του, αυτή δεν του έχει δοθεί, αφήνοντας ανοιχτή την πιθανότητα να διεξαχθεί η διαδικασία χωρίς τον απαραίτητο χρόνο ώστε να προετοιμαστεί η υπεράσπιση. Οι ποινές που αντιμετωπίζει ο υποψήφιος διδάκτορας φτάνουν μέχρι και την οριστική του διαγραφή. 


Τα δύο από τα τρία περιστατικά βασίζονται σε δικαστικές υποθέσεις για τις οποίες δεν έχει ξεκινήσει καν η δίκη, ενώ το τρίτο σε μια αναφορά φύλακα του κτηρίου Αβέρωφ.  Είναι αξιοσημείωτο ότι ένα από τα περιστατικά που βαραίνουν τον υποψήφιο διδάκτορα βασίζεται σε μήνυση που έχει καταθέσει ο πρύτανης ΕΜΠ για την συγκέντρωση στη “Βραδιά του Ερευνητή” το 2024, ο ίδιος πρύτανης που θα παρίσταται στο πειθαρχικό συμβούλιο. Πως νομιμοποιείται – τόσο τυπικά όσο και ηθικά – μια διαδικασία στην οποία δικαστής και μηνυτής συμπίπτουν; Στα υπόλοιπα περιστατικά, πρωταγωνιστούν η ιδιοκτήκτρια κυλικείου Γεωργία Τύρου και ο φύλακας του κτηρίου Αβέρωφ Γιώργος Τσουνιάς. Διάφορα στοιχεία, τα οποία παρατίθενται στο βίντεο και στην σχετική ανακοίνωση του σωματείου των ερευνητών, μπορούν να οδηγήσουν στο συμπέρασμα ότι τα εν λόγω άτομα αποτελούν “ευνοούμενους” του πρύτανη.


Το παρόν βίντεο εντάσσει την υπόθεση αυτή στο γενικότερο πλαίσιο της. 


Απέναντι στην καταστολή και στις σκευωρίες, απαντάμε με αλληλεγγύη και συλλογική αντίσταση!


Στις 7 Σεπτεμβρίου, συγκεντρωνόμαστε στις 17.00 έξω από την Πρυτανεία για να σταματήσουμε το πειθαρχικό – παρωδία!

content:
Oyuncu Serhat Kılıç, İstanbul Kağıthane’de yaşadığı evinde ölü bulundu. Kılıç’ın ölümüyle ilgili soruşturma başlatıldı.

Oyuncu Serhat Kılıç’tan perşembe gününden bu yana haber alamayan kız arkadaşı Özlem E. (50), Kılıç’ın yaşadığı eve geldi.

Özlem E., Kılıç’ı salondaki tekli koltukta oturur halde hareketsiz buldu. Kılıç’ın nefes almadığını ve vücudunun soğuk olduğunu fark eden Özlem E., 112’yi arayarak yardım istedi. İhbar üzerine adrese Kağıthane Asayiş Büro Amirliği ekipleri ile sağlık ekipleri sevk edildi. Sağlık ekiplerinin yaptığı kontrolde Kılıç’ın hayatını kaybettiği belirlendi.

Polisin bilgisine başvurduğu Özlem E., erkek arkadaşı Kılıç’ın lenf kanseri olduğunu, perşembe gününden bu yana kendisinden haber alamadığını söyledi. Polis ekipleri, Kılıç’ın ölümüyle ilgili soruşturma başlattı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Bayık: Democratization in Turkey and the resolution of the Kurdish issue are inextricably linked
content:
In the second part of an in-depth interview with ANF, Cemil Bayik, co-chair of the KCK (Kurdistan Communities Union) Executive Council, delves deeper into the current status and future course of the Peace and Democratic Society Process. He emphasizes, above all, the importance of not viewing the process solely from the perspective of the negotiating table, but rather that democratic forces must actively contribute at all levels. He also addresses the question of a possible roadmap for the process.


The first part of the interview can be read

here

.


How will the Peace and Democratic Society Process proceed? Does something like a roadmap for this process exist? Which kind of political steps do you expect to proceed in parallel with disarmament?


A law has been passed, but it still remains unclear how the process will proceed. The committee that includes Rêber Apo [Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan] and the committee chaired by the Vice President could clarify certain issues through discussion. The law passed makes implementation difficult. In fact, in some respects, it undermines the very purpose of the law. The law’s categorization of organization members – excluding the leadership and a significant number of further comrades – complicates the process. In a way, it runs itself into a standstill. This law has led to such a situation due to certain concerns of its own. Security concerns can be taken into account, but if matters are left to the security bureaucracy, situations will arise that stall the process. As a matter of fact, the sole focus on security from the state side so far has left the problem unsolved, and this has come at a high cost to Turkey.


A roadmap must be designed in such a way that it does not create any sense of insecurity. The healthy progress of the process and the solution itself require this. Our approach is clear and straightforward. We are not engaged in any games, stalling tactics, or the like. The government is well aware of this. However, the government’s hesitation – driven by various concerns – regarding the path and methods needed to ensure a roadmap functions effectively is preventing the process from moving forward quickly. In his latest statement, Rêber Apo noted that prolonging the process would provide a platform for those opposed to it. We share a similar perspective on this matter. Rêber Apo, in particular, is making great efforts to ensure the process moves forward quickly. However, the path and methods currently being pursued do not align with the nature of the process. On the one hand, there is talk of complete disarmament; on the other hand, a significant number of people are being excluded. It is clear that a situation where some are excluded and no sound or acceptable approach or method is proposed will not lead to progress. The leadership and a significant number of people will be excluded, yet demands will be made for certain actions to be taken… At the very least, this amounts to failing to recognize a movement that has been fighting for over 50 years. In short, approaching the law with a schematic and dogmatic mindset only complicates matters.


There is no “third party” institution in this process. This is a situation praised by government officials. Indeed, resolving the issue without needing such an institution is significant. However, the process must be carried out using methods and approaches that do not require the “third party” typically present in so-called conflict-resolution practices. It cannot be said that much attention is being paid to this at present. As the issue is not one that can be solved merely by laying down arms – and as the nature of a century-old problem is different – simply demanding that arms be laid down is no realistic approach.


As we have demonstrated our commitment to and practice of disarmament, their taking certain legal steps would accelerate the process. Our freedom movement has a clear commitment in this regard. It has demonstrated this so far and remains determined to demonstrate it even more clearly going forward. However, while the process needs to be accelerated by taking the necessary legal steps, there is a reluctance to do so. Parliament is viewed as the expression of the will of the Turkish people. This Parliament has predominantly emphasized that this issue will be resolved through democratization. It has also been clearly stated that the issue is the Kurdish question. author: Unknown
title: Karayılan calls on Kurdish organizations to develop a common strategy and national democratic unity
content:
Murat Karayılan, a member of the People’s Defense Center (HSM) Command, sent a video message to the 34th International Kurdish Culture Festival which kicked off in the German city of Dortmund earlier today.


Drawing particular attention to the current process, Karayılan stressed that: “Armed struggle has played its role in the Kurdish freedom struggle. From now on, we can achieve results through democratic politics.”


Karayılan’s message reads as follows:


“Dear people, esteemed friends, I extend my greetings and respects to you all.


On behalf of the leadership of our Movement, I congratulate you all on the 34th Kurdish Culture Festival and wish you success.


Thirty-four years ago, I was also in Europe, and it was decided at that time to organize such a festival. Since then, you have continued to hold it every year as a tradition. This is a highly valuable and meaningful stance against assimilation and cultural destruction.


At the same time, this festival was also announced as an occasion to commemorate the heroic martyrs. This, too, is valuable and meaningful. We thank and congratulate you for maintaining this stance.


Dear friends,


As you know, our struggle—the Kurdistan Freedom Struggle—is currently going through a very important, sensitive, and historic process. With the historic call of Leader Apo [Abdullah Öcalan] on February 27, 2025, our struggle entered a new era. This is a period of transition from a strategy of armed struggle to a strategy of democratic politics.


As people from Kurdistan living in Europe, you are closely following this process. To date, you have devoted tremendous effort to our struggle and made highly significant contributions. We hope that your efforts and participation will continue just as strongly in this new era.


It should be understood that Leader Apo initiated this new process with the aim of paving the way for success. We, as the Movement, also believe in this process. Armed struggle has played its role in the Kurdistan freedom struggle. From now on, we can achieve results through democratic politics.


The most important issue in advancing this new process is Leader Apo’s physical freedom. For all our comrades and the guerrillas, this is an indispensable condition. Leader Apo must be free and must personally lead this process. If this does not happen, the process cannot succeed.


Esteemed patriots,


We are an experienced movement. This process also carries certain risks. Therefore, we must proceed carefully and cautiously. In other words, both as a Movement and as a people, we must approach this period in this way. Nothing concrete has emerged yet. Leader Apo has defined this period as a period of struggle. We must all approach it as a process of struggle.


The Turkish state pursued a policy of denial against the Kurdish people. Every demand for rights put forward by our people was regarded as a rebellion and met with force and repression in an attempt to suppress it. Our revolutionary struggle was likewise described as a rebellion. For nearly 50 years, numerous methods and means have been employed in an effort to crush and eliminate our Movement. Particularly over the past 10 years, they sought to destroy us with NATO’s assistance, the support of certain regional powers, and the use of all kinds of modern and prohibited weapons.


Against these attacks aimed at our destruction, the Kurdistan Freedom Guerrilla waged historic resistance. They resisted in a spirit of self-sacrifice. Ultimately, they could neither destroy nor defeat us; we remained standing. It was then that the state turned to Leader Apo. This process developed on that basis.


Undoubtedly, the heroic martyrs have played an immense role in this. The resistance of Leader Apo and the heroic martyrs has played the fundamental role in bringing this process to where it is today.


Esteemed patriots,


For 53 years, a solid foundation has been built for the Kurdistan freedom struggle to achieve success. None of this came easily; it was achieved through hard work, sacrifice, and resistance. These gains were made possible through the resistance of our entire people and the efforts of Kurds in Europe.


Now, for a people to survive and achieve success, two fundamental elements are necessary:


The first is to develop a strategy—that is, strategic leadership.


The second is to create its own heroes.


No society that has created its heroes and developed its strategy can be defeated. Today, both of these …

author: Unknown
title: Selahattin Demirtaş: Selçuk Mızraklı will be released on September 8
content:
Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) former Co-Chair Selahattin Demirtaş shared a post on social media announcing that Selçuk Mızraklı, former Co-Mayor of Diyarbakır Metropolitan Municipality, will be released. Both politicians are jailed at Edirne High-Security Closed Prison in western Turkey and have been held in the same cell for the past four and a half years.


Demirtaş shared the following message: “Dr. Adnan Selçuk Mızraklı, the kind-hearted sage who has served seven years in prison in return for four months as mayor of Diyarbakır, will be released on Tuesday, September 8, having completed his sentence.”


Demirtaş added: “For the past five years, I have been entrusted to him, and he has been entrusted to me. He will walk out of here on Tuesday morning and be at Diyarbakır Airport that evening. From then on, he is entrusted to you. Eight letters, from the inside to the outside: ‘FREEDOM.’ The master is about to complete the crossword puzzle.”


Politician and doctor Selçuk Mızraklı was arrested in October 2019 while serving as the Co-Mayor of Diyarbakır Metropolitan Municipality and was replaced by a state-appointed trustee five months after his election. He has been imprisoned since.


Selahattin Demirtaş was imprisoned in connection with the Kobane protests in October 2014. Dozens of people were killed during the brutal crackdown on the nationwide unrest that broke out at the time against the Turkish government's support for the terrorist militia “Islamic State” (ISIS). In a subsequent trial, Demirtaş was sentenced to a total of 42 years in prison. He has been held in the high-security prison in Edirne since 2016.

author: Caitlyn Clark
title: Tyson Shutters Illinois Meatpacking Plant and Fires 2,500 Workers Without Notice
content:
Workers say both the company and their own union, United Food and Commercial Workers, hung them out to dry.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Ouano Tante worked the afternoon shift at the Tyson beef plant in Joslin, Illinois, for five years. But when she and hundreds of her co-workers arrived at work on August 14, they found the plant closed.

They speculated that someone on the morning shift might have gotten injured. Then two mid-level supervisors came outside in tears. Plant supervisors told workers the plant was closing permanently, effective immediately.

Inside, the early-morning shift had just ended when the workers were informed it would be their last. The cafeteria erupted into chaos. Plant supervisors stood guard by the doors, workers said, while everyone received their closure paperwork.

“People were crying, shaking,” Tante said. “When we were leaving the parking lot, there were so many car accidents. People were so upset.”

“They gave no reason, nothing,” said Ahoro Asselissime. “People have no job. No money to pay our bills. For 11 years, I made money for them. And now they’re not doing anything for me.”

Joslin is home to just 56 residents. But 2,500 workers from Africa, Latin America, and Burma toiled at the meatpacking plant there, butchering cattle for Tyson, one of the world’s largest meatpacking companies. The workers were represented by United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 1546.

Most of the workers live in the Quad Cities, clustered around the Illinois-Iowa border 160 miles west of Chicago. Everyone there knows someone who works at Tyson, the area’s ninth-largest employer. The closure announcement sent the community into a tailspin.

Tante, originally from Togo, had the job of determining the age of cattle by checking the size of their teeth. An overhead conveyor would move carcasses, suspended by their ankles, along the chain. Tante checked the teeth, sprinted up a set of stairs to mark the cattle’s ankles with ink, then sprinted back down to catch the next carcass.

Simultaneously, other workers drained blood from the animal by slicing the neck with knives. If Tante didn’t work fast enough or was off-pace with the other workers, she said, she could get cut by their knives.

The laid-off workers will be paid for 36 hours a week until October, but that’s far less than they had been making with overtime.

“I got $500 this week,” said Asselissime. “My rent is $925. I have to put gas in my car, buy food for my kids. Everything is so expensive now.” Prior to the closure, Asselissime could expect around $900 a week.

“I’ve been sounding the alarm about how Tyson treats their workers for years,” said Nana Ouro-Agoro, founder of Akwaaba, a nonprofit organization that provides support to the Quad Cities’ immigrant population.

Originally from Togo, Ouro-Agoro came to the Quad Cities after winning the immigration lottery in 2008. She learned that many of her neighbors worked at Tyson, where they were frequently injured on the job and afraid to speak out. Workers told her they were being treated “worse than the cattle.”

“It was hard for me to sleep at night, hearing my fellow immigrants were working hard, getting injured, and nothing was being done,” she said.

Akwaaba helped Tyson workers with translation services and resources to help them assert their rights, including when Tyson abruptly fired dozens of Togolese workers as alleged retaliation for reporting injuries and sexual harassment. Now, about 500 of their clients — roughly 1 in 4 — are out of work.

And because so much of the local economy depends on income from Tyson workers, “we’re going to see a crisis in every sector,” Ouro-Agoro said.

It’s been a profitable few years for Tyson. So why shutter the plant? Tyson cites the nationwide cattle shortage.

Cattle stock in the United States is at a 75-year low. The costs of raising cattle have gone up significantly for ranchers, in part due to drought and higher prices for fertilizer and diesel, exacerbated by the war on Iran.

But the crisis facing Tyson workers and cattle ranchers alike is driven by one major factor: corporate consolidation. The “Big Four” — Tyson, Cargill, JBS, and National Beef — own over 80 percent of the U.S. beef industry.

The Big Four have, according to multiple court decisions, colluded to fix prices for just about everything, from the price …

author: Nayanika Guha
title: Yup’ik Immersion School Program in Alaska Opens Doors to Cultural Connection
content:
Other Indigenous groups are looking to the K-8 language immersion program in Anchorage, Alaska, as an inspiring model.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Growing up in Bethel, Alaska, Amber Arnaqulluk Shields spoke Yup’ik from a very young age. Whenever she wasn’t in school, her parents sent her to their ancestral home in Toksook Bay to spend time with grandparents who spoke no English.

Speaking Yu’pik at home had always been a priority for her family, and so when Shields had her kids, whom she is raising in Anchorage, Alaska, she wanted to give them the same access to her culture and family connections. Her son Kangrilnguq, a rising fifth grader who is the eldest of her three children, was raised speaking Yup’ik.

“We only speak Yup’ik in the house to our kids. My son actually didn’t really know much English by the time he was in kindergarten,” Shields told Truthout.

However, she started noticing that Kangrilnguq would shy away from playing with other kids at the park and not want to meet any other kids outside the family. She recalls a time when she was helping her relatives move, and there was a child her son’s age there whom she was encouraging him to play with, but he refused and ran away to hide in their truck. “I was like, ‘Hmm, I wonder why he’s not paying with the kids.’ And I asked that little girl [in Yup’ik], ‘Hey, could you go into the back of my truck and help me get that bag out?’ And he jumped out of the truck, and he asked me, ‘Does she understand? She speaks Yup’ik?’” That’s when he started playing with her, and when it clicked for Shields that he wasn’t playing with other kids because they weren’t understanding each other.

As a result, when Shields learned about the Yup’ik immersion program at College Gate Elementary School in Anchorage, it was a natural choice for her to send her children there. Her son started the program as a kindergartener in 2022, “and my hope was that he’ll be able to understand his teachers, and his teachers would be able to understand him,” Shields said.

The program at College Gate started in 2018, with support from a federal grant, to reinvigorate Indigenous languages. Each year since its inception, the school has successfully added a grade to the program, and the Anchorage school system is now adding an 8th grade class to the program at Wendler Middle School, with plans to add high school grades next year, too.

“Kids are fully immersed with the target language for half the day, and then they get their reading and math for the other half with an English partner teacher,” explained Darrell Berntsen, the principal at College Gate Elementary. “And so that happens daily, where they’re with one teacher for the start of the day, and then they move to another teacher to end the day.”

It’s not just the language that is taught, Berntsen said — the culture is taught also. “So it has really changed the culture of my school … and our school has kind of adopted their culture because we act like a big village here at the school.”

The program at College Gate started in 2018, with support from a federal grant, to reinvigorate Indigenous languages.

According to Shields, this has been especially important for her family, and her son specifically. Their family engages in many Yup’ik subsistence practices “even though we’re in Anchorage,” Shields explained, and now her son is “able to feel normal, I guess, because there’s other kids that do subsistence.” In the Yup’ik immersion program, he can also regularly interact with Yup’ik elders who teach in the program. She recalls a time when their family was going to Bethel and had plans to go ptarmigan hunting, and Kangrilnguq promised to bring a bird back as gift for his teacher. Another time, she recalls he wanted to go fishing so that he could bring back fish for his teachers. “He’s like, ‘she’s an elder, and I want to give her fish.’ So we were able to still practice giving to elders that way, and he really appreciates being able to understand his teachers, his teachers being able to understand him and who he is and where he comes from.”

Berntsen, who is Alutiiq from Kodiak Island, said he hopes that the school’s Yup’ik immersion program will have a lasting effect on the city, and “that they’ll be able to kind of revive the language and have more Indigenous speakers here in Anchorage.” In 2018, Anchorage Daily News …

author: Nick Fulton
title: Trump’s “Beautification” Plan Has Turned Community Parks Into Policing Traps
content:
Trump’s plan to “make D.C. beautiful again” means more policing for the city’s residents.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The expenditures are enormous: $16 million toward a failed paint job on the National Mall reflecting pool. $5 million for bronze horse statues. Over $900 million toward White House renovations. Trump’s plans to “make D.C. beautiful again” are costing taxpayers well over a billion dollars and leaving local community members wondering who the renovations are really for.

These forced renovations by the administration are affecting more than landmarks and monuments. In Washington, D.C., a large portion of community parks are governed by the National Park Service and are included in federal land. These parks have become ground zero for local resistance to Trump’s hasty makeover of the District.

Malcolm X Park, also known as Meridian Hill Park, is located in Washington, D.C.’s Ward 1, one of the most diverse and densely populated wards in the city. The park has been a historic hub for organizing, public service, and unifying community gatherings. The park’s namesake came from Malcolm X’s history of organizing at the green space; in 1969, four years after his passing, Black activists including Angela Davis called for the park to be named in his honor.

In recent months, the park has fallen under federal siege. In August, Trump’s National Guard deployments, dubbed “Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful,” turned a year old. Since the federal takeover, about 9,700 troops from across the country have been dispatched to the nation’s capital, and around 4,600 were deployed across D.C. as of August 3. In addition to the presence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the National Park Police, and other policing agencies, the National Guard has turned once beautiful green spaces into militarized traps.

“[The parks] are federal property, so federal laws apply. And federal law is different from D.C. law on some things,” said Alex Dodds, campaign director and co-founder of Free DC, a fiscally sponsored project of Community Change that advocates for the dignity of the residents of D.C. FreeDC has also used Malcolm X Park as a hub for organizing a resistance movement to the Trump administration’s expanded project of policing.

“We have seen several instances over the last year during this time of dramatically aggressive federal policing, where people are getting arrested for basically having a picnic,” Dodds told Truthout.

Since Trump’s return to office, federal police have increased arrests for public consumption of alcohol (open containers) and open-air cannabis use in community parks. In D.C., possession and consumption of cannabis is decriminalized on private property. While it is not legal to use cannabis in public in D.C., the consequences are much more minimal than federal law mandates. Public use of cannabis according to local law is classified as a misdemeanor and could result in a citation. But federally, cannabis remains illegal and classified as a controlled substance, and possessing any amount of cannabis on federal land can land you a year in prison on the first offense. You can cross a street in D.C. and pass between these jurisdictions, making it easier for federal police to take advantage of these confusing legal differences in favor of harsher penalties.

“We have seen several instances over the last year during this time of dramatically aggressive federal policing, where people are getting arrested for basically having a picnic.”

This increase in policing and punishment goes beyond marijuana possession or a bottle of wine, too. Under Trump’s “beautification” plans and aggressive immigration policies, U.S. Park Police have been coordinating with ICE to support deportation efforts in public spaces. Between September 2025 and February 2026, court records show at least 10 instances where a person was arrested by ICE for immigration reasons but with the involvement and support of a U.S. Park Police officer in the metro D.C. area, according to Maryland Matters.

According to community leaders, these policing partnerships have created an environment that makes public spaces in D.C. feel unsafe.
